full_text: ABSTRACTThe Amapa State, Brazil, in the Amazon region and bordering French Guiana, is a strategic sentinel location for infectious disease surveillance. Ecological pressures such as deforestation, artisanal gold mining, and high human mobility contribute to complex transmission dynamics of arboviruses, bacterial infections, and other pathogens. This study aims to characterize the etiologies of acute febrile illness (AFI) reported in Amapa State in 2018-2020, focusing on arbovirus circulation, bacterial contributions, and emerging pathogens. A retrospective analysis was carried out with 727 AFI cases. Laboratory diagnoses were established using molecular and serological assays, with systematic testing for different pathogens. Definitive diagnoses were obtained in 185 individuals (25.4%), yielding 209 positive results and including 23 cases of co-infection. Dengue virus was the predominant etiological agent (n=109, 52%), followed by leptospirosis (n=20, 9.5%), chikungunya virus (n=16, 7.6%), parvovirus B19 (n=16, 7.6%), measles (n=15, 7.1%), zika virus (n=10, 4.8%), mayaro virus (n=1,0.5%), and other bacterial infections (n=5, 2.4%). Isolated cases of hepatitis A and B, malaria, SARS-CoV-2, enterovirus, and acute Chagas disease were also identified. No hepatitis E virus or oropouche cases were detected. Dengue virus was the leading cause of AFI. Leptospirosis, chikungunya virus, and parvovirus B19 were other prevalent and often underrecognized contributors. The detection of additional viruses highlights Amapa State as a potential zone of “silent expansion” for emerging arboviruses. Co-detection of multiple pathogens underscores diagnostic complexity in regions with overlapping transmission. Strengthening surveillance, expanding laboratory capacity, and prioritizing differential diagnostics are essential to capture epidemiological dynamics and guide public health interventions.KEYWORDS: Dengue, Leptospirosis, Arbovirus infections, Chikungunya fever, Parvovirus B19 MATERIAL AND METHODSStudy design and populationAn observational, cross-sectional, retrospective, and descriptive study was conducted using a convenience sample. Serum specimens were collected from patients presenting with AFI during routine diagnostic procedures in public health laboratories. Samples from 727 individuals, collected in 2018 (n = 20), 2019 (n = 581), and 2020 (n = 126), were analyzed.This study aims to find the potential etiologies of viral and other infections in AFI cases reported from 2018 to 2022 in the Amazon region of Amapa State, Brazil. AFI, with a fever duration cutoff of 2-7 day from onset, was chosen as the inclusion criterion.Laboratory proceduresSpecimens were initially processed at the Central Public Health Laboratory of Amapa State (LACEN-AP) following routine diagnostic protocols, including arbovirus screening when clinically indicated. Additional tests, such as serology and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for other pathogens, were performed at the discretion of attending physicians, with results recorded on GAL. Confirmatory local methods included enzyme linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) for immunoglobulin M (IgM) and NS1 (the latter exclusively for dengue), electrochemiluminescence, reverse transcription PCR (RT-PCR), and sequencing; for bacterial and fungal infections, ELISA for leptospirosis and blood, urine, and stool cultures were performed; whereas parasitic infections were confirmed using thick blood smears, the Strout test, electrochemiluminescence, and immunochromatographic tests.After initial processing, samples were stored at −20 °C and shipped to the Virology Laboratory of the Institute of Tropical Medicine of Sao Paulo, Faculty of Medicine, University of Sao Paulo (LV-IMT-FMUSP, LIM-52), in which they were preserved at −80 °C until further testing.Molecular screeningAt LV-IMT-FMUSP, samples underwent real-time PCR assays targeting viral agents. The screening included assays for Pan-Orthoflavivirus and Pan-Alphavirus. The following viral agents were tested: Flaviviruses, Alphaviruses, Orthobunyaviruses: yellow fever 8 , dengue, zika, chikungunya, mayaro, and oropouche viruses 9 .Genus Orthoflavivirus 10 : Japanese encephalitis, Russian spring-summer encephalitis, tick-borne encephalitis, Usutu, West Nile, and Saint Louis encephalitis viruses.Genus Alphavirus 11 : Ross River, O’nyong-nyong, Sindbis, Barmah Forest, Eastern equine encephalitis, Western equine encephalitis, and Venezuelan equine encephalitis viruses. Additional real-time PCR assays included pathogens with overlapping clinical presentations, such as enterovirus 12 , parvovirus B19 13 , hepatitis E virus (HEV) 14 , and Leptospira spp 15 .GALIn this study, diagnostic test results from LACEN-AP were retrieved via GAL.GAL, the national computerized system, was designed to manage and monitor laboratory routines within the National Public Health Laboratory Network. It is managed by the Ministry of Health via the General Coordination of Public Health Laboratories and tracks the flow of biological samples from collection to final diagnosis, standardizing results and providing real-time data for the surveillance of high-priority and compulsory notification diseases.SINANSINAN, the primary national surveillance database managed by the Brazilian Ministry of Health, is a decentralized system fed by the mandatory notification of diseases and conditions in the National Compulsory Notification List.SINAN provides high-resolution microdata (individual-level records) that include clinical and demographic variables (age, sex, pregnancy status, municipality of residence, reported condition, date of symptom onset, and clinical manifestations), diagnostic test results, among others.Integration of dataClinical and demographic variables (age, sex, municipality of residence, reported condition, date of symptom onset, and clinical manifestations) were combined with GAL laboratory results. Using this integrated dataset, data analysis was strictly descriptive, focusing on characterizing the reported cases.For the diagnostic tests either at LACEN or IMT, samples were classified as positive if they were reactive in at least one assay.Statistical analysisContinuous variables are shown as medians and interquartile ranges (IQR), and categorical ones, as frequencies. Subgroup pairwise comparisons were performed via the Pearson’s chi-square or Fisher’s exact tests. Correlation between monthly cases and NASA POWER precipitation data was assessed using Spearman’s rank test. The Benjamini-Hochberg procedure was applied to control the false discovery rate across multiple comparisons. Spatial distribution maps were generated using the geobr, sf, and ggplot2 packages. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05, using R(version 4.4.0) via RStudio. full_text_sections.discussion: DISCUSSIONThis study investigated the etiologies of AFI cases reported in Amapa State from 2018 to 2022. Of 727 evaluated individuals, definitive diagnoses established 185 cases (25.4%), including 23 cases of co-infection.Our findings are in line with previous regional studies. Dengue remains the predominant AFI etiological agent in Latin America, with chikungunya and zika showing an increased prevalence. Leptospirosis, though often overlooked, represents a prevalent bacterial contributor1,16.Notably, this study found one case of mayaro virus infection, consistent with its rare occurrence in Amapa State (six confirmed cases nationwide in 2015-2025) 17 . Following systematic PCR testing, no individual in our cohort was positive for Oropouche virus disease, despite epidemiological data (2015-2025) reporting 16,571 cases nationwide, including 218 in Amapa State. A recent increase in its detection (2023-2024) likely reflects greater diagnostic capacity and active case-finding 17 . These results suggest Amapa State may represent a zone of “silent expansion” for Oropouche virus disease, in which overlapping arbovirus transmission obscures true disease burden. Strengthening surveillance, expanding laboratory capacity, and prioritizing differential diagnostics are essential to capture epidemiological dynamics and guide interventions. While multiplex syndromic panels are ideal, widespread molecular testing faces strict budget and logistical constraints within the public health system in Amapa State. A more sustainable solution could be a tiered “reflex testing” cascade at LACEN-AP. Under this protocol, a negative molecular result for primary arboviruses (dengue/zika/chikungunya) would automatically trigger reflex testing for leptospirosis and parvovirus B19 using the original biological sample. This flow could optimize laboratory resources, cut costs, and bypass initial clinical triage blind spots without requiring secondary patient appointments. Lessons from the Amazon highlight the global importance of integrated arbovirus surveillance in regions with overlapping transmission.The fact that 80.5% of initial hypotheses were generically classified as suspected arboviruses exposes a profound “dengue-centric” bias. Because the early symptoms of dengue, parvovirus B19, and leptospirosis overlap almost entirely, physical triage alone is insufficient. To address this, the regional health system must implement targeted continuing medical education focusing on broad syndromic classifications—such as “acute exanthematous febrile syndrome”—rather than single-pathogen guessing. Furthermore, standard patient intake forms should mandate structured epidemiological risk questions regarding recent floodwater exposure (leptospirosis), mining or forest exposure (malaria/arboviruses), and artisanal acai consumption (acute Chagas disease) to guide clinical suspicion before laboratory results are available.Leptospirosis remains a critical public health challenge in Amapa State linked to seasonal flooding, precarious sanitation, and transmission in wetland and stilt-house communities 18 , 19 . Despite its prevalence, underreporting persists due to symptomatic overlap with malaria and dengue 20 . Our finding that Leptospira spp. was the second most prevalent confirmed pathogen underscores its critical standing in the regional etiology of AFI. Unlike arboviral infections, which only require supportive care, leptospirosis demands timely antibiotic therapy to prevent severe, potentially fatal complications such as Weil’s disease or pulmonary hemorrhage syndrome. Relying entirely on early clinical differentiation or waiting days for laboratory confirmation in highly endemic zones often results in catastrophic therapeutic delays. Therefore, in areas with high dengue and leptospirosis co-endemicity, clinical protocols must explicitly support the initiation of empirical antibiotic treatment (such as doxycycline or amoxicillin) for patients presenting with severe febrile syndromes and clear epidemiological risk factors, prioritizing clinical survival over definitive laboratory timelines.Parvovirus B19 occurred in 16 cases (7.6%), representing a notable proportion of AFI diagnoses. Its clinical recognition remains challenging as its early symptoms closely mimic arboviruses such as dengue, Zika, and chikungunya. In tropical regions, B19V is often misdiagnosed as dengue due to overlapping presentations of fever, headache, and rash 21 , 22 . The post-pandemic resurgence of B19V in 2024-2025 marked a significant epidemiological shift driven by an “immunity gap” in pediatric populations. IgM positivity peaked at ~40% in children aged 5-9 years and ~10% in adults, complicating AFI differential diagnosis 23 .Of the 727 investigated individuals, viral hepatitis was suspected in 10 cases (1.4%), with three confirmed cases of hepatitis A and B (1.4%). No HEV cases were identified despite evidence that HEV genotype 3 is a zoonotic pathogen of concern in Brazil 24 , 25 .Meta-analyses estimate anti-HEV IgG seroprevalence at ~6% nationally, with regional variations: ~3% in the Amazon and up to 14.2% in rural Rondônia 26 - 28 . Diagnostic invisibility remains a major challenge as public health screening routinely ignores HEV testing, particularly in vulnerable Amazonian populations. Overlapping clinical presentations with hepatitis b and d further obscure HEV detection, suggesting that some acute hepatitis cases of “unknown etiology” may represent undiagnosed HEV.Measles occurred in 15 cases (7.1%). Despite mass vaccination programs, Brazil lost its measles-free status in 2018 following outbreaks linked to Venezuelan migration and low vaccination coverage 29 , 30 . Although elimination status was regained in 2023-2024, new cases in Tocantins in 2025 highlight ongoing vulnerability. The porous border of Amapa State with French Guiana and high mobility of illegal gold miners create a unique epidemiological corridor sustaining measles and other infectious diseases.Malaria transmission remains a major concern in Oiapoque, one of the highest transmission zones in the Americas. Despite persistent “silent” transmission by asymptomatic carriers in mobile populations, our cohort only included two malaria cases (0.95%), reflecting the predominance of samples collected in Macapa. Epidemiological data shows a downward trend in Amapa State, with a 16.8% reduction in cases from 2024 to 2025 and an 82% decline in Macapa. Nonetheless, the Oiapoque border remains the main epidemiological challenge in the state 31 - 34 . The cohort included a case of acute Chagas disease, reflecting the specific epidemiological profile of Amapa State. From 2018 to 2022, the state remained a high-endemicity region for acute Chagas disease in the Brazilian Amazon, with oral transmission—primarily by consumption of artisanal acai and bacaba juice—emerging as the dominant route of infection 35 , 36 .A notable finding in this study was the elevated detection of multiple infectious agents. Across 727 patients, this study found 209 reactive results, with co-detection of distinct pathogens in 23 cases. Similar patterns have been reported in regions endemic for malaria and arboviruses, in which simultaneous infections are confirmed by multiple molecular assays 37 , 38 . In such contexts, potential cross-reactivity further compounds diagnostic complexity. The cross-reactivity between zika, dengue, and yellow fever serological assays, for example, is primarily attributed to the high degree of structural homology within the envelope protein in members of the Orthoflavivirus genus 39 .The seasonal transmission pattern in this study likely reflects the equatorial climate of the region, in which persistently high precipitation and elevated temperatures sustain vector breeding sites throughout the year. Thus, the continuous circulation of febrile illnesses in Amapa State may obscure the more distinct seasonal peaks and lag patterns in other climatic se…
full_text_sections.conclusion: CONCLUSIONSThe causes of AFI in Amapa are multiple and may involve infection by more than one etiological agent. This underscores the complexity of diagnostic accuracy in regions with overlapping multiple arbovirus and bacterial transmission. The detection of rare pathogens such as Mayaro virus and acute Chagas disease reflects the unique ecological and epidemiological profile of the region. These findings reinforce the role of Amapa State as a sentinel for infectious disease surveillance as its porous borders, ecological connectivity, and high human mobility sustain transmission corridors. Strengthening laboratory capacity, integrating differential diagnostics, and expanding surveillance systems are essential to capture the true burden of AFI and to guide targeted interventions. While acknowledging the limitations inherent to retrospective designs and diagnostic constraints, this study emphasizes the global relevance of integrated surveillance in ecologically dynamic regions. Crucially, addressing these challenges requires improving data completeness, such as by the meticulous entry and digital optimization of GAL forms, to ensure accurate epidemiological tracking in complex equatorial settings.
full_text_sections.other: INTRODUCTIONManaging the prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of community-acquired acute febrile illness (AFI) constitutes a major public health challenge in Latin America due to its complex epidemiological profile and potentially profound social consequences 1 . A comprehensive understanding of their etiologies is essential for advancing clinical practice, guiding public health strategies, and informing policy development.The ecology of the Amazon basin—characterized by deforestation, flooding, and high vector diversity—creates favorable conditions for arboviruses and bacterial pathogens, amplifying the risk of febrile outbreaks 2 . Thus, the region experiences a wide spectrum of febrile illnesses caused by viral, bacterial, and parasitic agents, reflecting diverse ecological and climatic conditions 3 .The overlapping clinical manifestations of diseases such as dengue, malaria, leptospirosis, and rickettsial infections complicate accurate diagnosis. This diagnostic uncertainty often results in delayed or inappropriate treatment. Misdiagnosis may postpone life-saving antibiotic therapy, whereas indiscriminate prescribing contributes to antimicrobial resistance. The Pan American Health Organization 4 has emphasized antimicrobial resistance as a regional priority, highlighting its impact on healthcare costs and mortality.Community-acquired AFI contributes substantially to regional morbidity and mortality, considerably straining healthcare systems and requiring significant resource allocation for surveillance and management. Socioeconomic factors, including poverty and limited access to healthcare, exacerbate transmission dynamics and hinder effective disease control 5 .Surveillance represents a critical component of disease control. The Brazilian Amazon is recognized as a global hotspot for emerging viruses 2 . Integrated screening systems may serve as sentinel mechanisms for early detection. As deforestation and mining activities intensify, human populations increasingly encounter novel vectors such as mosquitoes and midges, underscoring the importance of screening febrile patients for malaria and arboviruses6. Without routine screening, outbreaks may remain undetected, manifesting themselves only as “unexplained fevers.”Amapa State, in the Eastern Brazilian Amazon, exemplifies one of the most complex diagnostic environments in the world. While dengue remains a major concern, the unique geography of the state—bordering French Guiana and the Atlantic Ocean, and dominated by dense rainforest and wetlands—heightens the risk of diverse infectious diseases. High rainfall and humidity render leptospirosis endemic, particularly in peri-urban areas such as Macapa and Santana 5 . Recent land-use transformations, including illegal mining and the expansion of acai production, have had measurable epidemiological consequences. These activities are consistently associated with increased malaria incidence due to favorable conditions for Anopheles vectors 6 . Moreover, the commercialization of acai has contributed to the emergence of foodborne transmission of Chagas disease 7 .EthicsThis study was approved by the institutional Research Ethics Committee (CAAE No 53153916.7.0000.0065). All data were anonymized prior to analysis, and access to secondary data from the Laboratory Environment Manager (GAL) and the Notifiable Diseases Information System (SINAN) was restricted to variables necessary for epidemiological characterization (with authorization from health surveillance authorities). EthicsThis study was approved by the institutional Research Ethics Committee (CAAE No 53153916.7.0000.0065). All data were anonymized prior to analysis, and access to secondary data from the Laboratory Environment Manager (GAL) and the Notifiable Diseases Information System (SINAN) was restricted to variables necessary for epidemiological characterization (with authorization from health surveillance authorities). Laboratory proceduresSpecimens were initially processed at the Central Public Health Laboratory of Amapa State (LACEN-AP) following routine diagnostic protocols, including arbovirus screening when clinically indicated. Additional tests, such as serology and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for other pathogens, were performed at the discretion of attending physicians, with results recorded on GAL. Confirmatory local methods included enzyme linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) for immunoglobulin M (IgM) and NS1 (the latter exclusively for dengue), electrochemiluminescence, reverse transcription PCR (RT-PCR), and sequencing; for bacterial and fungal infections, ELISA for leptospirosis and blood, urine, and stool cultures were performed; whereas parasitic infections were confirmed using thick blood smears, the Strout test, electrochemiluminescence, and immunochromatographic tests.After initial processing, samples were stored at −20 °C and shipped to the Virology Laboratory of the Institute of Tropical Medicine of Sao Paulo, Faculty of Medicine, University of Sao Paulo (LV-IMT-FMUSP, LIM-52), in which they were preserved at −80 °C until further testing. Molecular screeningAt LV-IMT-FMUSP, samples underwent real-time PCR assays targeting viral agents. The screening included assays for Pan-Orthoflavivirus and Pan-Alphavirus. The following viral agents were tested: Flaviviruses, Alphaviruses, Orthobunyaviruses: yellow fever 8 , dengue, zika, chikungunya, mayaro, and oropouche viruses 9 .Genus Orthoflavivirus 10 : Japanese encephalitis, Russian spring-summer encephalitis, tick-borne encephalitis, Usutu, West Nile, and Saint Louis encephalitis viruses.Genus Alphavirus 11 : Ross River, O’nyong-nyong, Sindbis, Barmah Forest, Eastern equine encephalitis, Western equine encephalitis, and Venezuelan equine encephalitis viruses. Additional real-time PCR assays included pathogens with overlapping clinical presentations, such as enterovirus 12 , parvovirus B19 13 , hepatitis E virus (HEV) 14 , and Leptospira spp 15 . GALIn this study, diagnostic test results from LACEN-AP were retrieved via GAL.GAL, the national computerized system, was designed to manage and monitor laboratory routines within the National Public Health Laboratory Network. It is managed by the Ministry of Health via the General Coordination of Public Health Laboratories and tracks the flow of biological samples from collection to final diagnosis, standardizing results and providing real-time data for the surveillance of high-priority and compulsory notification diseases. SINANSINAN, the primary national surveillance database managed by the Brazilian Ministry of Health, is a decentralized system fed by the mandatory notification of diseases and conditions in the National Compulsory Notification List.SINAN provides high-resolution microdata (individual-level records) that include clinical and demographic variables (age, sex, pregnancy status, municipality of residence, reported condition, date of symptom onset, and clinical manifestations), diagnostic test results, among others. Integration of dataClinical and demographic variables (age, sex, municipality of residence, reported condition, date of symptom onset, and clinical manifestations) were combined with GAL laboratory results. Using this integrated dataset, data analysis was strictly descriptive, focusing on characterizing the reported cases.For the diagnostic tests either at LACEN or IMT, samples were classified as positive if they were reactive in at least one assay. title_original: Sentinel surveillance of acute febrile illness in a Brazilian Amazon region: laboratory findings and epidemiological implications

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to identify the potential etiologies of viral and other infections in acute febrile illness (AFI) cases reported from 2018 to 2022 in the Amazon region of Amapa State, Brazil, to better understand the epidemiological landscape of these infections.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study was a sentinel surveillance conducted in public health laboratories in the Amazon region of Amapa State, Brazil, from 2018 to 2022, analyzing samples from 727 individuals. Definitive diagnoses were obtained in 185 individuals (25.4%), yielding 209 positive results and including 23 cases of co-infection.
analysis.methods: Diagnostic tests included serology, polymerase chain reaction (PCR), and sequencing, with results recorded on GAL. Confirmatory methods at the Virology Laboratory of the Institute of Tropical Medicine of Sao Paulo (LV-IMT-FMUSP) involved enzyme linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), electrochemiluminescence, reverse transcription PCR (RT-PCR), and sequencing for viral agents, while bacterial and fungal infections were confirmed using cultures and other specific tests.
analysis.main_results: Measles was identified as one of the pathogens with 15 positive results out of 53 tests (28.3%). Other notable findings included dengue (109/650, 16.8%), leptospirosis (20/98, 20.4%), chikungunya (16/86, 18.6%), and parvovirus B19 (16/21, 76.2%). There were 23 cases of co-infection, with measles being involved in 7 cases.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted these findings as highlighting the significant role of measles virus in the etiology of acute febrile illness in the region, contributing to the understanding of the disease burden and the need for targeted surveillance and control measures.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform public health strategies for measles surveillance and control in the Amazon region, emphasizing the importance of integrating laboratory data with clinical and demographic information to better manage and prevent outbreaks.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's descriptive analysis may limit the depth of interpretation, and the statistical significance of some findings was affected by the Benjamini-Hochberg correction, suggesting moderate evidence strength for the observed associations.

analysis.summary_en: This study conducted sentinel surveillance of acute febrile illness (AFI) in the Amazon region of Amapa State, Brazil, from 2018 to 2022, identifying measles virus as a significant etiological agent. Measles was detected in 15 out of 53 tests (28.3%), with 7 cases of co-infection involving dengue. The study combined clinical and demographic data with laboratory results from GAL and LV-IMT-FMUSP, using methods such as ELISA, RT-PCR, and sequencing. While the findings highlight the role of measles in the region's AFI cases, the descriptive nature of the analysis and the impact of statistical corrections on some results suggest moderate evidence strength. These results can inform public health strategies for measles surveillance and control in the area.

title: Integrated Immune Profiling Identifies Treatment-Associated Immune Patterns in Patients with B‐Cell Hematological Malignancies

full_text: AbstractImmune dysfunction in hematological malignancies arises from both disease-related alterations and therapeutic interventions, yet comprehensive approaches for characterizing the immune status remain limited. We evaluated an integrated immune profiling strategy combining antigen-specific serology and high-dimensional B-cell phenotyping. Thirty-eight patients with B-cell hematological malignancies receiving ibrutinib-, lenalidomide-, and rituximab-based therapies, or no treatment, were analyzed. Antigen-specific humoral responses were assessed by using a customized protein microarray containing 37 microbial antigens, enabling parallel IgG and IgM profiling. B-cell subpopulations were characterized by spectral flow cytometry. Multiomics factor analysis was applied to integrate serological and cellular data sets and identify major sources of immune variability. Distinct serological and cellular immune profiles were observed across therapeutic groups. Patients receiving ibrutinib displayed lower IgG levels against several microbial antigens and alterations in multiple B-cell compartments, whereas patients receiving lenalidomide-based therapy showed comparatively preserved B-cell populations and broader antigen-specific IgG reactivity. Rituximab-containing regimens were associated with marked reductions in several B-cell subsets. Integrated analysis identified cellular immune features as the major contributors to interpatient heterogeneity, which suggests the presence of treatment-associated immune patterns within the studied cohort. Therefore, integrated serological and cellular profiling provides a scalable framework for characterizing an immune fingerprint with potential prognostic value in patients with B-cell hematological malignancies. These findings support further investigation of immune monitoring approaches in larger longitudinal cohorts.Keywords: oncohematological malignancies, integrated immune profiling, immunocompetence, humoral immune dysfunction, cellular immunophenotyping, multiomics factor analysis, treatment-associated immune signatures 2.MaterialsEthanol 96%, 3-(2-aminoethylamino)-propyldimethoxymethylsilane (MANAE) (≥95.0%), bis­(sulfosuccinimidyl)­suberate (BS3), glycerol 85%, bovine serum albumin (BSA), fetal bovine serum (FBS), Tween 20, dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), Hybriwell sealing system, Grace Bio-Laboratories ProPlate microarray system, Grace Bio-Laboratories ProPlate clips for microarray systems (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis/MO, USA), SuperBlock Tris-buffered saline (#37535), Pierce bicinchoninic acid Protein Assay Kit (#23225), Blocker BSA (10%) in phosphate buffered saline (PBS) (#37525), microscope slides (76 × 26 mm), Mseries Lifterlip y Lifterslip coverslips, Live/Dead Fixable Blue Dead Cell Stain Kit, Gibco RPMI 1640 Medium (Thermo Scientific, Rockford/IL, USA), Microarray-Specific 384-well Microplates, Optimum Microarray Printing Buffer C (ArrayJet, Roslin, UK), Streptavidin-Fluor Cy3 Cytiva Amersham, Cytiva Ficoll–Paque PLUS (Cytiva 17–1440–03) (GE-Healthcare, Little Chalfont, Buckinghamshire, UK), Cy3-AffiniPure Donkey Anti-Human IgG (cat. no. 709–165–149), Alexa Fluor 647-AffiniPure Goat Anti-Human IgM (cat. no. 109–605–043) (Jackson ImmunoResearch, Ely, UK), Brilliant Stain Buffer (#563794) (BD Biosciences, San Jose, CA), and True-Stain Monocyte Blocker (#426101) (BioLegend, San Diego, CA) were used. The mAgs included in the array are listed in Table S1, and the antibodies used for B-cell immunophenotyping are listed in Table S2.2.1.Equipment and SoftwareArrayJet Printer Marathon v1.4, JetSpyder 12 samples, JetStar (ArrayJet, Roslin, UK), Scanner SensoSpot Fluorescence (Miltenyi Imaging GmbH, Radolfzell, Germany), GenePix 4000B Microarray Scanner, GenePix Pro Microarray Analysis Software (Axon, Molecular Devices, San Jose, CA, USA), Orbital shaker (FALC Instruments S.r.l.; Treviglio, Italy), Fisherbrand Microplate Vortex Mixers (Fisherbrand, EEUU), Digital Dry Block Heater (Thermo Scientific, Rockford/IL, USA), 5-laser Aurora spectral cytometer (Cytek Biosciences, CA, USA), R statistics software (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria. http://www.R-project.org/), Infinicyt software (version 2.1.0.a.000; BD Biosciences, San Jose, CA) were used. 4.1.Humoral Immune Profile in Oncohematological PatientsTo characterize antigen-specific antibody profiles across therapeutic groups, an exhaustive characterization of the humoral profile was performed. While a distinct serological profile is observed among the different groups (Figure ), PCA revealed that the heterogeneity in mAg profiles was not fully explained only by the treatment (Figure S4). High variations in IgG levels have been observed in the analysis of the different therapies (Figures and S5). Figure A shows that there was a distinct serological profile between treated vs nontreated individuals. Lower levels of IgG against mAgs from Cytomegalovirus, measles virus, SARS-CoV-2, and varicella-zoster were consistently observed in treated patients, regardless of the administered treatment (Figure B). In addition, the volcano plots revealed differences across each treatment modality in the IgG profile (Figure C). Among the key findings, levels of IgG antibody against Norovirus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and SARS-CoV-2 antigens were significantly elevated in lenalidomide- or rituximab-based treatments, compared with ibrutinib (Figure D). Interestingly, the IgM serological profile did not differ among the distinct groups, except for the S. pneumoniae antigen (Figures S6 and S7). Levels of this IgM antibody were higher in patients treated with rituximab, which may reflect a distinct effect on early immune responses to bacterial infections in comparison with other therapies.1Effect of different treatment modalities on the IgG profiles. (A) Volcano plot displaying the statistical significance of Z-score ratios (X-axis) between treated and nontreated patients. Statistical differences between groups were assessed using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test (Y-axis). The mAgs with statistically significant differences are highlighted in blue dots. (B) Boxplots of the IgG humoral profile comparing treated and nontreated patients. Boxplots show the median (horizontal line) and interquartile range (box). Yellow represents patients with treatment, and pink represents those with no treatment. Statistical differences between groups were assessed using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test (p-value: * <0.05; ** <0.01). (C) Volcano plots highlighting the statistical significance of Z-score ratios between ibrutinib, lenalidomide, and rituximab. Each volcano plot represents the comparison between treatment modalities. (D) Boxplots of the IgG humoral profile against mAgs according to treatment. Each color represents a different group: green for ibrutinib, orange for lenalidomide, purple for rituximab, and pink for no treatment.Together, these findings revealed treatment-associated differences in serological profiles against common mAgs and may be useful for immune monitoring. While these findings suggested a treatment-associated impairment of humoral immunity (potentially affecting vaccine-induced immunity), clinical factors, such as age and sex, may also contribute to the observed variability in immune responses. The reduced IgG levels observed in ibrutinib-treated patients may, therefore, reflect a combined effect of therapy and host-related factors, suggesting reduced serological responses against previously encountered pathogens. This highlights the importance of monitoring potential reactivation of infections or increased susceptibility to new ones, given their compromised immune status due to the impairment of the immune response. These findings suggest that monitoring humoral immunity during treatments containing ibrutinib may facilitate infection risk assessment and support preventive clinical strategies. full_text_sections.abstract: AbstractImmune dysfunction in hematological malignancies arises from both disease-related alterations and therapeutic interventions, yet comprehensive approaches for characterizing the immune status remain limited. We evaluated an integrated immune profiling strategy combining antigen-specific serology and high-dimensional B-cell phenotyping. Thirty-eight patients with B-cell hematological malignancies receiving ibrutinib-, lenalidomide-, and rituximab-based therapies, or no treatment, were analyzed. Antigen-specific humoral responses were assessed by using a customized protein microarray containing 37 microbial antigens, enabling parallel IgG and IgM profiling. B-cell subpopulations were characterized by spectral flow cytometry. Multiomics factor analysis was applied to integrate serological and cellular data sets and identify major sources of immune variability. Distinct serological and cellular immune profiles were observed across therapeutic groups. Patients receiving ibrutinib displayed lower IgG levels against several microbial antigens and alterations in multiple B-cell compartments, whereas patients receiving lenalidomide-based therapy showed comparatively preserved B-cell populations and broader antigen-specific IgG reactivity. Rituximab-containing regimens were associated with marked reductions in several B-cell subsets. Integrated analysis identified cellular immune features as the major contributors to interpatient heterogeneity, which suggests the presence of treatment-associated immune patterns within the studied cohort. Therefore, integrated serological and cellular profiling provides a scalable framework for characterizing an immune fingerprint with potential prognostic value in patients with B-cell hematological malignancies. These findings support further investigation of immune monitoring approaches in larger longitudinal cohorts.Keywords: oncohematological malignancies, integrated immune profiling, immunocompetence, humoral immune dysfunction, cellular immunophenotyping, multiomics factor analysis, treatment-associated immune signatures

full_text_sections.discussion: 5.DiscussionOur study provides an integrated characterization of serological and B-cell immune profiles in patients with B-cell hematological malignancies receiving different therapeutic regimens, including ibrutinib-, lenalidomide-, and rituximab-containing treatments. Distinct serological and cellular immune patterns were observed across the therapeutic groups, highlighting the heterogeneity of immune alterations and immune status of these patients. Since both the underlying disease and treatment can influence humoral and cellular immunity (particularly B-cell subpopulations and antigen-specific antibody responses), a comprehensive assessment of immune status is revealed by an integration of serological profiling with high-dimensional B-cell immunophenotyping.As might be expected, distinct patient subgroups exhibited heterogeneous serological profiles defined by the presence of IgM and IgG antibodies against common mAgs. These serological profiles offer important insights into how serological immunity markers and immune dysregulation may influence disease evolution and infection susceptibility. Understanding pathogen-specific antibody profiles in individuals with reported previous infections may provide valuable information for guiding clinical management of these patients. This has been considered particularly important in infections such as SARS-CoV-2, as it may influence the course of the infection, vaccine efficacy, and hospitalizations. Additionally, it has been demonstrated that some individuals are more prone to reinfection, highlighting the importance of understanding the impact of prior infections and long-lasting antibody responses. Our results reveal how the B-cell compartment is differentially reshaped beyond the antitumoral treatments (ibrutinib-, lenalidomide-, or rituximab-based therapies), because of distinct observed effects on B-cell differentiation, activation, and effector function. Patients receiving lenalidomide-based therapies displayed comparatively higher frequencies of pre–GC B-cells, MBC, and PB subpopulations, together with stronger IgG responses against viruses primarily affecting the respiratory and/or gastrointestinal tracts. These findings are consistent with the immunomodulatory role of lenalidomide, resulting in more effective antigen-dependent B-cell differentiation and comparatively preserved humoral responses. In contrast, Rituximab-based therapies were associated with profound remodeling of the B-cell compartment due to depletion of CD20+ B-cells. Despite this, these patients retained a relatively strong capacity to mount immune responses against multiple mAgs and exhibited a selective increase in IgM reactivity to S. pneumoniae, consistent with the known increased infection risk reported in the literature caused by the depletion of B-cells and the associated impaired humoral immunity. ,− These observations underscore the importance of detailed infection surveillance and tailored preventive strategies in the population undergoing therapy.Ibrutinib-treated patients showed lower IgG responses against several mAgs (including Norovirus, S. pneumoniae, SARS-CoV-2, and Varicella-Zoster virus) together with reduced frequencies of pre-GC B-cells, MBCs, and PBs, suggesting altered B-cell activation and differentiation. These findings are consistent with the known effects of Bruton’s tyrosine kinase inhibition on B-cell receptor signaling and humoral immune responses, ,− as well as the increased risk for opportunistic infections. , In addition, changes in memory B-cell subsets, including reduced frequencies of DN1 (associated with long-lived immune protection) and a relative increase in pro-inflammatory DN2/DN3 populations, may reflect alterations in B-cell homeostasis previously associated with inflammatory and activated immune states. − Collectively, these observations suggest that treatments containing ibrutinib compromise both antibody production and long-term immunity, which may contribute to impaired humoral responses to infections and vaccination. − Overall, the data showed that ibrutinib- and rituximab-containing regimens were associated with reduced frequencies in B-cell subpopulations, whereas lenalidomide-based treatments better preserve the total number of B-cells, highlighting distinct immunological fingerprints associated with each therapy. These effects on cell activation, exhaustion, and isotype switching might present clinical implications for infection risk, vaccine responses, and long-term humoral immunity. Therefore, these therapies can induce profound immune dysregulation through cell depletion, exhaustion, altered tumor microenvironment, and incomplete immune reconstitution. ,− These findings underscore the value of integrative multiomics approaches to disentangle the relative contributions of cellular and humoral immunity to global immune status in oncohematological patients. The predominance of B-cell immunophenotypic features as the principal driver of variance suggested that alterations within the cellular compartment may represent a more sensitive indicator of immune perturbation than humoral immune profiles. While antigen-specific IgM and IgG responses contributed substantially to the integrated model, they explained less heterogeneity, reinforcing that antibody titers alone may not fully capture immune heterogeneity during therapy. From a translational perspective, the strong discriminative performance observedparticularly associated with lenalidomidesuggests distinct therapy-associated immune patterns. Therefore, integrated immune signatures could serve as potential biomarkers of treatment exposure requiring further validation.The integration of serological signatures with B-cell immunophenotypic profiles presents prognostic potential and could provide novel insights into the biology of the diseases; however, our study is limited in several aspects. The cohort was relatively small, predominantly composed of CLL patients, and treatment groups were closely associated with specific disease entities. Furthermore, the lack of age- and sex-matched healthy controls, the cross-sectional study design, the absence of functional immune assays, and the lack of external validation of the ROC analyses limited the transferability of the results. Despite these limitations, the comprehensive serological and immunophenotypic characterization presented here offers valuable insights into immune dysregulation following the treatment. Future longitudinal studies in larger and more diverse cohorts, complemented by functional immune analyses, will be essential to validate these observations, define the dynamics of immune recovery over time, and determine their clinical outcomes. Importantly, to our knowledge, this is the first study to provide an integrated framework combining high-dimensional serological profiling with detailed B-cell immunophenotyping in a clinically relevant cohort of patients with B-cell hematological malignancies. This multidimensional approach establishes a foundation for future biomarker discovery and precision immune monitoring, aimed at improving patient stratification and therapeutic decision-making.
full_text_sections.conclusion: 6.ConclusionsImmune dysfunction is a hallmark of oncohematological diseases, shaped by both the underlying disease and treatments such as ibrutinib- and rituximab-containing regimens. Evaluation of pathogen-specific antibody profiles and B-cell immunophenotypes may provide valuable information for immune monitoring and warrants further investigation in larger prospective cohorts. These approaches could support personalized clinical strategies, including vaccination before immunosuppressive treatment, monitoring pathogen-specific IgM and IgG levels, and considering alternative therapies to mitigate the infectious risk.This study offers an initial immune fingerprint of oncohematological patients across different treatment regimens and highlights the importance of comprehensive immune assessment at diagnosis and prior to therapy. Such an evaluation may enable risk-adapted, personalized treatment decisions and improved monitoring of infections in immunocompromised patients.
full_text_sections.other: 1.IntroductionHematological malignancies comprise a highly heterogeneous group of diseases affecting the blood, bone marrow, and lymphoid organs, which are characterized by widely variable prognoses and a high rate of relapse. They account for 1.2 million new cases worldwide each year, representing about 7% of all newly diagnosed cancers. Lymphoid malignancies, including lymphomas, leukemias, and multiple myeloma (MM), are characterized by clonal proliferation of immune cells and exhibit substantial biological and clinical heterogeneity. Non-Hodgkin lymphomas (NHLs) arise from mature lymphocytes at different stages of differentiation and encompass indolent to highly aggressive forms, each requiring distinct therapeutic strategies. Despite major advances in treatment, including targeted therapies and immunotherapies, many patients fail to respond or eventually develop resistance, highlighting an unresolved challenge in disease management. Follicular lymphoma (FL) is a typically slow-growing, indolent B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder arising from follicular center B-cells. It commonly presents with widespread lymphadenopathy, bone marrow involvement, and splenomegaly and less commonly other extranodal sites. FL is the second most common type of NHL, representing about 30%. , Leukemias originate from hematopoietic cells in the bone marrow and lead to the accumulation of abnormal blood cells. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), one of the most common leukemias, is defined by the expansion of CD5+ B-cells and profound immune dysregulation. Malignant B-cells in CLL show resistance to apoptosis and impaired immune activity, resulting in both humoral and cellular immune dysfunction. , Additionally, CLL is also associated with significantly altered T-cell function, which compromises antitumor immunity and increases susceptibility to infections. , Currently, several therapeutic options are available for leukemias and lymphomas, such as chemotherapy, monoclonal antibodies (i.e., rituximab), kinase inhibitors (i.e., ibrutinib), and advanced cellular therapies such as CAR-T cells. , Although these therapeutic approaches have substantially improved patient outcomes, therapeutic resistance remains a major limitation for these pathologies.MM is characterized by clonal expansion of plasma cells in the bone marrow and has benefited from treatments such as proteasome inhibitors, immunomodulatory drugs like lenalidomide, monoclonal antibodies, and autologous stem cell transplantation. Nevertheless, the disease remains largely incurable, particularly in advanced stages. Increasing evidence indicates that MM therapies are associated with significant immune alterations, leading to an increased risk of infections, including bacterial, viral, and opportunistic infections and reactivation of latent pathogens. , Infections represent a major complication in these onco-hematologic malignancies due to disease-related immune dysregulation and treatment-induced immunosuppression. In CLL patients, viral infections may act as a triggering factor in the early stages of the disease, potentially promoting clonal expansion through chronic antigenic stimulation. Patients with MM, NHL, and FL also show increased susceptibility to infections due to impaired antibody production and T-cell dysfunction, further exacerbated by therapies such as chemotherapy and targeted agents. ,, The infection severity and resolution (with or without sequelae) are influenced by the immune resilience and immunocompetence of the patient, which encompasses mechanisms that restore immune function and maintain self-tolerance. , Immunological memory generated by previous infection or vaccination can mitigate reinfections and reduce severity. − Humoral immunity, mediated by antibodies produced by B-cells, is crucial. B-cells constitute a heterogeneous population of functionally distinct phenotypic subsets well-defined by their maturation status and immunophenotype expression, each contributing differently to antibody production, immune memory, and pathogen neutralization. − In these pathologies, functional B-cells are often depleted or replaced by malignant clones, reducing the ability to sustain effective responses. , Consequently, immune protection and vaccine-induced immunity are highly variable among patients and are influenced by disease stage, tumor burden, and immune impairment. , Currently, the relative impact of several antitumor therapies on humoral and cellular immune responses, particularly in these oncohematological diseases, remains poorly defined and not well understood. Although targeted therapies are designed to reduce secondary effects, these patients often present intrinsic immune dysfunctions. , Immunosuppression is observed with the initiation of the treatment and disease progression due to cumulative therapeutic exposure. , Therefore, early prognosis might be crucial to enable risk-adapted treatment strategies and improve the prevention of infections. Our aim is to characterize antigen-specific humoral responses of patients with oncohematological malignancies undergoing different therapeutic regimens (containing ibrutinib, lenalidomide, or rituximab). For this purpose, serological profiling using a functional antigen microarray was employed to assess their immune response against 37 common microbial antigens (mAgs), and B-cell immunophenotyping was carried out by spectral flow cytometry. title_original: Integrated Immune Profiling Identifies Treatment-Associated Immune Patterns in Patients with B‐Cell Hematological Malignancies

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to evaluate an integrated immune profiling strategy to identify treatment-associated immune patterns in patients with B-cell hematological malignancies, addressing the need to understand how different therapies affect immune responses.
analysis.study_design_and_population: An integrated analysis was conducted on patients with B-cell hematological malignancies, comparing immune profiles across treatment groups including ibrutinib, lenalidomide-based therapy, rituximab-containing regimens, and no treatment. The study identified cellular immune features as major contributors to interpatient heterogeneity.
analysis.methods: Antigen-specific humoral responses were assessed using a customized protein microarray with 37 microbial antigens for parallel IgG and IgM profiling. Statistical differences between groups were evaluated using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test. B-cell subpopulations were analyzed via PCA and correlation analysis.
analysis.main_results: Patients receiving ibrutinib showed lower IgG levels against several microbial antigens and alterations in multiple B-cell compartments. Lenalidomide-based therapy preserved B-cell populations and showed broader antigen-specific IgG reactivity. Rituximab-containing regimens were associated with marked reductions in several B-cell subsets. The volcano plots revealed differences in IgG profiles across treatment modalities, with significant elevations in IgG against Norovirus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and SARS-CoV-2 antigens in lenalidomide- or rituximab-based treatments compared with ibrutinib.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that treatment-associated differences in immune profiles can be identified, highlighting the potential for immune monitoring to assess infection risk and support preventive strategies.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results may inform immune monitoring approaches in clinical settings, aiding in the assessment of infection risk and the development of preventive strategies for patients undergoing specific therapies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's findings are based on a single cohort and may not be fully generalizable. The evidence is moderate, as the observed heterogeneity in immune profiles was not entirely explained by treatment alone, and the study did not account for all potential confounding factors.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated treatment-associated immune patterns in patients with B-cell hematological malignancies using an integrated immune profiling approach. The objective was to evaluate how different therapies, such as ibrutinib, lenalidomide-based therapy, and rituximab-containing regimens, affect immune responses. The methods included antigen-specific serology using a customized protein microarray and B-cell phenotyping via immunophenotyping and PCA. The main results showed that ibrutinib reduced IgG levels against several microbial antigens and altered B-cell compartments, while lenalidomide-based therapy preserved B-cell populations and broadened antigen-specific IgG reactivity. Rituximab regimens led to marked reductions in B-cell subsets. The findings suggest that immune monitoring during treatment could help assess infection risk and guide preventive strategies. However, the study's evidence is moderate due to its focus on a single cohort and the potential influence of confounding factors such as age and sex on immune variability.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在评估综合免疫分析策略,以确定 B 细胞血液恶性肿瘤患者中与 治疗 相关的免疫模式,解决了解不同疗法如何影响 免疫应答 的需要。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 对 B 细胞血液恶性肿瘤患者进行了综合分析,比较了 治疗 组的免疫特征,包括依鲁替尼、基于来那度胺的治疗、含利妥昔单抗的治疗方案和无 治疗 的治疗方案。该研究确定细胞免疫特征是患者间异质性的主要贡献者。
elements_zh.methods: 使用具有 37 种微生物抗原的定制蛋白质微阵列来评估抗原特异性体液反应,以进行平行 IgG 和 IgM 分析。使用 Wilcoxon 秩和检验评估组间的统计差异。通过 PCA 和相关分析对 B 细胞亚群进行分析。
elements_zh.main_results: 接受依鲁替尼治疗的患者针对多种微生物抗原的 IgG 水平较低,并且多个 B 细胞区室发生变化。基于来那度胺的疗法保留了 B 细胞群,并显示出更广泛的抗原特异性 IgG 反应性。含利妥昔单抗的治疗方案与几种 B 细胞亚群的显着减少有关。火山图揭示了 治疗 模式中 IgG 谱的差异,与依鲁替尼相比,基于来那度胺或利妥昔单抗的 治疗 中针对诺如病毒、肺炎链球菌和 SARS-CoV-2 抗原的 IgG 显着升高。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究结果表明,可以识别与 治疗 相关的免疫特征差异,凸显了免疫监测评估感染风险和支持预防策略的潜力。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些结果可以为临床环境中的免疫监测方法提供信息,帮助评估感染风险并为接受特定治疗的患者制定预防策略。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究的结果基于单个 队列研究,可能无法完全推广。证据是中等的,因为观察到的免疫特征的异质性不能完全用 治疗 单独解释,而且该研究没有考虑所有潜在的混杂因素。

full_text: AbstractIntroductionRubella infection during pregnancy poses significant risks, including congenital rubella syndrome (CRS), miscarriage, and fetal death. Vaccination programs have reduced rubella incidence globally, but regional differences in coverage and immunity persist. The objective of the study was to assess the seroprevalence of anti-rubella IgM and IgG antibodies among pregnant women in South-Western Romania, with a focus on temporal trends, demographic factors, and the impact of vaccination eligibility.MethodsThis observational, cross-sectional study included pregnant women screened for TORCH infections at the County Clinical Emergency Hospital of Craiova, Romania, during two periods: 2013–2016 and 2019–2022. Serum samples were tested for anti-rubella IgM and IgG antibodies. Participants were stratified by age, area of residence (rural/urban), and eligibility for rubella vaccination based on birth year.ResultsA total of 3,268 samples were analyzed. The seroprevalence of acute rubella infection (IgM positive) was low and slightly decreased from 0.54% (2013–2016) to 0.50% (2019–2022), with the most notable decrease in rural areas and among women aged 21–25 years. The overall seroprevalence of protective IgG antibodies was stable (88.28% vs. 88.91%), but remained below the WHO target of 95%. IgG seroprevalence increased among the youngest (<20 years) and 31–35 years age groups, particularly in rural areas, suggesting improved vaccination coverage and natural immunity from past outbreaks. Mapping in Dolj County revealed high seroprevalence near major cities.DiscussionDespite improvements, the relatively low IgG seroprevalence in South-Western Romania highlights the need to reinforce vaccination campaigns, especially in rural areas and among family physicians. Enhanced education and access to vaccination are essential to achieve the WHO eradication target and prevent CRS.Keywords: antibodies, congenital infections, pregnant women, rubella, seroprevalence studies 2.Material and methods2.1.Study design and participantsThis observational, cross-sectional study included pregnant women from South-Western Romania who presented for routine TORCH screening at the Gynecology Department of the County Clinical Emergency Hospital of Craiova, Romania. Two study periods were analyzed (2013–2016 and 2019–2022). In the first period, 368 women were tested for IgM and 367 for IgG, compared with 2,779 and 2,669 women, respectively, in the second period. Not all participants were tested for both antibodies: some women were tested only for IgM or only for IgG as part of routine clinical care, which explains the difference between the number of women tested for each antibody; no additional exclusion criteria were applied beyond having at least one valid rubella serology result.2.2.Sample size calculationAccording to the National Institute of Statistics, the South-Western (Oltenia) region of Romania had 974,202 women of childbearing age (15–49 years) in 2019 (9). Using the lowest regional rubella IgG seroprevalence reported in Romania at the time of study design (91.4%) (10), we estimated that a minimum sample of 121 pregnant women would be required to estimate seroprevalence with a two-sided 95% confidence interval and a ± 5% margin of error, using the standard formula n = Z2p(1−p)/d2 (Z = 1.96). The achieved sample sizes for IgG testing (367 in Group 1 and 2,669 in Group 2) exceeded this minimum, corresponding to margins of error of approximately ±2.87% and ±1.06%, respectively; the smaller Group 1 sample therefore yields comparatively less precise estimates, a point considered further in the Limitations.2.3.Data collection and variablesFor each participant, demographic data including age and area of residence (urban or rural) were recorded, together with the results of anti-rubella IgM and IgG serological testing.2.4.Laboratory testingPregnant women were screened during the first trimester of pregnancy as part of routine prenatal care.Between 2013 and 2016, anti-rubella IgM and IgG antibodies were measured using an electrochemiluminescence immunoassay (ECLIA) on the Cobas e601 analyzer (Roche Diagnostics, Basel, Switzerland). Between 2019 and 2022, serological testing was performed using a chemiluminescent microparticle immunoassay on the Architect i1000 system (Abbott Laboratories, Abbott Park, IL, USA) with original reagents. Both platforms report anti-rubella IgG results in international units per milliliter, calibrated against the WHO International Standard for anti-rubella immunoglobulin. However, multicentric evaluations of commercial rubella IgG immunoassays, including these two platforms, have shown that quantitative titers and, to a lesser extent, qualitative classification near the assay cut-off may differ between platforms despite this common calibration (11). This potential source of inter-assay variability should be considered when interpreting between-period comparisons and is discussed further in the Limitations.2.5.Statistical analysisData were exported from the hospital electronic database (HIPOCRATE) and analyzed using STATA version 17 (StataCorp LLC, College Station, Texas, USA). Continuous variables were expressed as mean ± standard deviation, while categorical variables were reported as counts and percentages.Comparisons between the two study periods were performed using the chi-square test for categorical variables. Differences in mean age between groups were assessed using the Student's t-test, as age was normally distributed. A p-value <0.05 was considered statistically significant.Because this is a cross-sectional study, associations between vaccination-eligibility cohorts (or area of residence) and antibody seroprevalence are expressed as prevalence ratios (PR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI), rather than risk ratios, in line with recommended practice for prevalence (rather than incidence or risk) data (12). PR estimates were calculated as the ratio of the crude prevalence in each comparison subgroup to that of the reference subgroup (women born before 1989, not eligible for rubella vaccination), with 95% CIs derived using the standard log-linear approximation and a continuity correction (+0.5) applied to comparisons involving zero-count cells.IgM seropositivity was interpreted descriptively as a possible marker of recent or acute rubella infection and was not used to estimate population-level rubella immunity; a positive IgM result alone does not equate to confirmed acute infection, since definitive confirmation would require IgG avidity testing or reverse-transcription PCR, both of which were outside the scope of this cross-sectional serological survey.2.6.Vaccination eligibility cohortsParticipants were stratified into four subgroups based on year of birth as a proxy for eligibility for rubella vaccination in Romania, in accordance with the national immunization schedule (Table 1).Table 1Correspondence between birth year and eligibility for rubella vaccine in Romania.Birth year<19891989199019911992199319941995199619971998199920002001200220032004200520062007Age group G126–3021–2521–2521–2521–25<20<20<20<20<20<20–––––––––Age group G231–3526–3026–3026–3026–3026–3021–2521–2521–2521–2521–25<20<20<20<20<20<20–––Eligible RCVNOYESD1YESD1YESD1YESD1YESD1YESD1–––––––––––––Eligible MMRNONONONONONONONONOYES D2YES D2YES D2YES D2YES D2YES D2YES D1 + 2YES D1 + 2YES D1 + 2YES D1 + 2YES D1 + 2D1, one dose of RCV vaccine.D2, second dose of MMR vaccine.D1 + 2: both doses of MMR vaccine.Women born before 1989 were considered non-eligible for rubella vaccination, as they were older than 15 years at the time of introduction of the rubella-containing vaccine in 2003. Women born between 1989 and 1994 were eligible for the monovalent rubella-containing vaccine (RCV) administered to adolescent girls between 2003 and 2008. Women born between 1995 and 1996 constituted a vaccination gap cohort, as they were not eligible for either the RCV program or the childhood MMR schedule. Women born in 1997 or later were considered eligible for the MMR vaccine; those born between 1997 and 2002 received only the second MMR dose, while those born from 2003 onward were eligible for both doses.Women born between 1997 and 2002, listed in Table 1 as eligible only for the second MMR dose, received a first dose of monovalent measles vaccine (without a rubella component) in infancy, before the MMR vaccine replaced it in the national immunization schedule in 2004; their first exposure to a rubella-containing vaccine therefore occurred with the second MMR dose, administered at 6–7 years of age, typically as a school-based catch-up dose (7, 10, 13). This is also the only birth cohort in this classification, together with the 1989–1994 RCV-eligible cohort, that received a rubella-containing vaccine as a single dose rather than the two-dose MMR schedule.2.7.Institutional review board statementThe study was conducted according to the ethical principles regarding human experimentation and clinical research, and was approved by the Committee of Ethics and Academic and Scientific Deontology, Craiova, Romania (approval no. 84/16.09.2020). 2.1.Study design and participantsThis observational, cross-sectional study included pregnant women from South-Western Romania who presented for routine TORCH screening at the Gynecology Department of the County Clinical Emergency Hospital of Craiova, Romania. Two study periods were analyzed (2013–2016 and 2019–2022). In the first period, 368 women were tested for IgM and 367 for IgG, compared with 2,779 and 2,669 women, respectively, in the second period. Not all participants were tested for both antibodies: some women were tested only for IgM or only for IgG as part of routine clinical care, which explains the difference between the number of women tested for each antibody; no additional exclusion criteria were applied beyond having at least one valid rubella serology result.
