full_text_sections.discussion: 4.DiscussionThis is the largest study performed in the South-West Romania regarding the seroprevalence of anti-Rubella antibodies in pregnant women, which came to complete the studies performed in other regions of Romania.We observed a decrease in the mean age of pregnant women that addressed for testing anti-Rubella antibodies, which can reflect a decrease in the mean age of pregnant women in general or better access to healthcare for young pregnant women.The increase of more than 7-fold in the number of pregnant women tested for anti-Rubella antibodies from 2013 to 2016 to 2019–2022 can be explained by the increase in medical information of patients and progress of laboratory technology associated with a reduction of testing costs, which become affordable for the average pregnant women (15, 16).Because the national immunization program for rubella was introduced in Romania in 2003 (8), we expect a higher proportion of tested women under 20 years of age to be IgG-positive.4.1.History of Rubella in RomaniaIn Romania, the first rubella cases were reported even since 1949 (17). In years 2002–2003, in Romania was recorded a large rubella outbreak (17), with over 115,000 reported cases, leading to an incidence rate of 531/100,000 inhabitants and 150 cases of suspected CRS, but only seven were confirmed. The epidemic affected mostly children, with an incidence rate of 2564/100,000 for the 5–9 years age group and 2446/100,000 in the 10–14 years age group.As response measures, in the absence of an RCV, was implemented an outbreak response plan that included surveillance for anti-rubella antibodies in the affected children of pregnant women who either had rubella disease or had a history of contact with a confirmed rubella case.This outbreak contributed to the acceleration of RCVs into the national vaccination programme.Between 2011 and 2012 another rubella outbreak occurred in Romania, with reported incidence rates of 20.6/100,000 inhabitants in 2011 and 97.5/100,000 inhabitants in 2012 (18). During the same period, 137 cases of CRS were reported. Most IgM positive cases were in the 15–19-year-old age group, and 97.7% of cases had no history of vaccination.4.2.Anti-Rubella IgM antibodies seroprevalenceGlobally, according to the CDC, the number of reported rubella cases has declined from 94,277 in 2012 to 10,194 in 2020 (19). The CRS showed an increased incidence from 302 reported cases in 2012 to 603 reported cases in 2020. This apparent increase in incidence was actually a reporting bias, as new countries with large populations (Bangladesh, India, Indonesia, and Pakistan) were included in the WHO surveillance network (19).In February 2020, 27 rubella cases were reported in six countries (Ireland, Germany, Italy, Poland, Portugal, and Norway), of which 18 were reported in Poland (20).In our study, the prevalence of anti-rubella IgM antibodies was 0.54% between 2013 and 2016 (2 cases) and 0.50% (14 cases) between 2019 and 2022 (Table 3). A similar seroprevalence (0.531%) was reported in a rubella outbreak in Romania in 2003 (17). In a study performed during the 2010–2011 rubella outbreak in Romania, 88 (28.02%) of 314 pregnant women tested positive for IgM (a marked difference from the low, inter-epidemic seroprevalence found in the present study, consistent with the much higher pre-test probability of true infection during an active community outbreak, as opposed to the low-prevalence, endemic setting of our cohorts, where a larger relative proportion of IgM-positive results are expected to be false positives; see below) (18). A study performed in the same period reported a peak prevalence of 10.525% among children under 14 years of age from urban areas in Northern Romania (21). Between 2008 and 2010 in the Banat region (Western Romania), a seroprevalence of 0.479% was reported among women of childbearing age, compared with 0.273% between 2015 and 2018 (22). The results of our study confirmed this descending trend in IgM seroprevalence from 0.54% between 2013 and 2016 and 0.50% between 2019 and 2022. The ECDC website reported only four rubella cases in Romania during 2019–2020 and no reported cases since 2021 (20).When interpreting the results of the IgM antibody test, we must consider the possibility of a false-positive result due to laboratory error. Even if modern methods for the detection of antibodies have high specificity, if many women are screened, there is a real possibility that some of the results are false positives (23). A study performed in the United States on pregnant women concluded that up to 11% of cases positive for IgM antibodies were actually negative (24). Also, is demonstrated cross reactivity between IgM anti-rubella antibodies and the rheumatoid factors that is present in blood in many auto-immune diseases (23).A false-positive IgM result was documented in samples collected from women infected with viruses, such as parvovirus B19, or those that were positive for rheumatoid factor (18, 23).4.3.Anti-Rubella IgG antibodies seroprevalenceThe seroprevalence of anti-Rubella IgG antibodies of 88.28% during 2013–2016 and 88.91% during 2019–2022 was rather low compared to the WHO target of 95% seroprevalence rate (19). Globally, seroprevalence rates as low as 53% have been reported (10). In Europe, a meta-analysis found 16 studies reporting a seronegativity rate > 10% (<90% seropositivity) (25). The lowest reported seroprevalence was 81.2% in pregnant women in Greece in 2006, and the highest was 98.6% in women of childbearing age in the Czech Republic (26). The WHO sets a goal of eradication of rubella in Europe by 2030 (27).Comparing the seroprevalences reported in our study with those reported in other regions of Romania, we observed that in Western Romania, higher seroprevalences were reported between 2008 and 2010 (94.1%) and 2015–2018 (91.5%) in women of childbearing age (22).We did not observe a significant change in the overall seroprevalence between the two time periods (88.28% vs. 88.91%; p = 0.721) (Table 4). If we consider the age group, we observed a non-significant increase in seroprevalence in young women aged < 20 years, from 78.57% between 2013 and 2016 to 85.11% between 2019 and 2022 (p = 0.362). This numerically higher (though not statistically significant) seroprevalence can be tentatively explained if we consider the eligibility for vaccination because women that had 15–20 years between 2013 and 2016 were born between 1993 and 2000, which was confirmed by studies in Western Romania (28). Those born between 1993 and 1994 were eligible for the RCV vaccine, those born between 1995 and 1996 were not eligible for either vaccine, and those born between 1997 and 2000 were eligible for the second dose of the MMR vaccine (Table 1). In contrast, pregnant women aged 15–20 years between 2019 and 2022 were born between 1999 and 2004 and were eligible for at least one dose of MMR vaccine (Table 1), which explains the higher seroprevalence. In this age group, the (non-significant) difference was numerically larger in urban areas (66.67% vs. 77.94%, p = 0.529) than in rural areas (81.82% vs. 87.38%, p = 0.462) (Table 4). Another age group in which we saw an increase in seroprevalence (from 82.50% to 92.42%) was 31–35 years. These women were not eligible for an RCV vaccine; thus, the increase in seroprevalence can be attributed to natural immunization. This could be due to two rubella outbreaks that occurred in Romania in 2003 and 2011–2012 (17, 18). A study performed in 1989 (29) showed a seroprevalence of 75.3% in this age group, whereas another study from Western Romania reported a seroprevalence in women aged 26–34–93.6% between 2008 and 2010 and 91.8% between 2015 and 2018. We can conclude that the seroprevalence is on an ascending trend in Romania from 1989 to 2022. This is despite governmental data showing a decrease in vaccination coverage from 93.2% in 2010 to 89.6% in the first dose and to 80.9% in the second dose in 2018 (2…
full_text_sections.conclusion: 5.ConclusionsThis study provides updated evidence on rubella immunity among pregnant women in South-Western Romania. Acute rubella infection was rare across both study periods, while overall anti-rubella IgG seroprevalence remained stable but consistently below the 95% threshold associated with WHO elimination targets. Although rural–urban differences diminished over time, population-level immunity remains insufficient to prevent congenital rubella syndrome.The identification of lower IgG seroprevalence in specific birth cohorts, particularly women born during the 1995–1996 vaccination gap and those born in the MMR-eligible era, highlights persistent immunity gaps despite long-standing vaccination programs. These findings suggest that vaccination eligibility alone does not guarantee adequate protection in women of reproductive age.Strengthening rubella prevention in South-Western Romania requires targeted catch-up vaccination strategies, enhanced counseling by family physicians, and sustained surveillance of susceptible cohorts. Addressing these immunity gaps is essential for achieving rubella and congenital rubella syndrome elimination goals.
full_text_sections.other: 1.IntroductionRubella is an airborne viral infection caused by the rubella virus, a Rubivirus in the family Matonaviridae (1) (reclassified from the former family Togaviridae following the 2018 ICTV taxonomy revision). Following the widespread introduction of rubella-containing vaccines (RCVs), global rubella incidence declined substantially, from over 670,000 reported cases in 2000 to fewer than 15,000 cases in 2018 (2). Nevertheless, rubella has not been eliminated, and sporadic cases continue to be reported in Europe, particularly in countries with suboptimal vaccination coverage (3).Although rubella is usually a mild, self-limiting disease in children and non-pregnant adults, maternal infection during pregnancy can result in severe adverse outcomes, including miscarriage, stillbirth, fetal death, and congenital rubella syndrome (CRS) (4, 5). The risk of CRS is strongly dependent on gestational age at infection, being highest during the first trimester and decreasing thereafter (5). For this reason, rubella immunity among women of childbearing age remains a critical public health concern, even in the post-vaccination era.CRS is a preventable condition characterized by permanent disabilities, most commonly sensorineural deafness, cardiac malformations, ocular abnormalities, and neurodevelopmental impairment (2, 5). The introduction of RCVs has dramatically reduced the global burden of CRS; however, immunity gaps persist where vaccine coverage is incomplete or heterogeneous. These gaps may remain undetected until susceptible women reach reproductive age, at which point the consequences of infection become clinically and socially significant.The World Health Organization (WHO) has set rubella and CRS elimination targets that require sustained high vaccination coverage, ideally exceeding 95% with rubella-containing vaccines (6). Despite progress, global RCV coverage was estimated at only 68% in 2022, and marked differences persist between regions and countries (7). In Europe, although two doses of the measles–mumps–rubella (MMR) vaccine are included in national immunization schedules, vaccination coverage remains uneven. Countries such as Romania and Poland continue to report lower coverage rates compared with Western European states (3).In Romania, rubella vaccination was introduced relatively late (Figure 1). A monovalent rubella-containing vaccine was administered to adolescent girls between 2003 and 2008, followed by the inclusion of the MMR vaccine in the childhood immunization program starting in 2004 (7, 8). As a result, several birth cohorts experienced incomplete or inconsistent vaccination exposure, creating potential immunity gaps that may persist into adulthood. Previous outbreaks in Romania, most notably in 2003 and 2011–2012, disproportionately affected these cohorts and highlighted the vulnerability of unprotected women of reproductive age.Figure 1History of vaccination anti-Rubella in Romania.Timeline graphic illustrating the introduction of vaccines in Romania’s national vaccination programme: Rubella-containing Vaccine in 2003 for children born 1989-1994, first MMR dose in 2004 for 2003-2007 births, and second MMR dose in 2005 for 1997-2002 births.Pregnant women represent a sentinel population for assessing population-level rubella immunity, as insufficient protection directly translates into the risk of CRS. However, contemporary seroprevalence data from South-Western Romania remain limited. The present study aimed to assess the seroprevalence of anti-rubella IgG and IgM antibodies among pregnant women over two distinct periods (2013–2016 and 2019–2022) and to identify immunity gaps according to age, area of residence, and vaccination eligibility cohorts. 2.2.Sample size calculationAccording to the National Institute of Statistics, the South-Western (Oltenia) region of Romania had 974,202 women of childbearing age (15–49 years) in 2019 (9). Using the lowest regional rubella IgG seroprevalence reported in Romania at the time of study design (91.4%) (10), we estimated that a minimum sample of 121 pregnant women would be required to estimate seroprevalence with a two-sided 95% confidence interval and a ± 5% margin of error, using the standard formula n = Z2p(1−p)/d2 (Z = 1.96). The achieved sample sizes for IgG testing (367 in Group 1 and 2,669 in Group 2) exceeded this minimum, corresponding to margins of error of approximately ±2.87% and ±1.06%, respectively; the smaller Group 1 sample therefore yields comparatively less precise estimates, a point considered further in the Limitations. 2.3.Data collection and variablesFor each participant, demographic data including age and area of residence (urban or rural) were recorded, together with the results of anti-rubella IgM and IgG serological testing. 2.4.Laboratory testingPregnant women were screened during the first trimester of pregnancy as part of routine prenatal care.Between 2013 and 2016, anti-rubella IgM and IgG antibodies were measured using an electrochemiluminescence immunoassay (ECLIA) on the Cobas e601 analyzer (Roche Diagnostics, Basel, Switzerland). Between 2019 and 2022, serological testing was performed using a chemiluminescent microparticle immunoassay on the Architect i1000 system (Abbott Laboratories, Abbott Park, IL, USA) with original reagents. Both platforms report anti-rubella IgG results in international units per milliliter, calibrated against the WHO International Standard for anti-rubella immunoglobulin. However, multicentric evaluations of commercial rubella IgG immunoassays, including these two platforms, have shown that quantitative titers and, to a lesser extent, qualitative classification near the assay cut-off may differ between platforms despite this common calibration (11). This potential source of inter-assay variability should be considered when interpreting between-period comparisons and is discussed further in the Limitations. 2.5.Statistical analysisData were exported from the hospital electronic database (HIPOCRATE) and analyzed using STATA version 17 (StataCorp LLC, College Station, Texas, USA). Continuous variables were expressed as mean ± standard deviation, while categorical variables were reported as counts and percentages.Comparisons between the two study periods were performed using the chi-square test for categorical variables. Differences in mean age between groups were assessed using the Student's t-test, as age was normally distributed. A p-value <0.05 was considered statistically significant.Because this is a cross-sectional study, associations between vaccination-eligibility cohorts (or area of residence) and antibody seroprevalence are expressed as prevalence ratios (PR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI), rather than risk ratios, in line with recommended practice for prevalence (rather than incidence or risk) data (12). PR estimates were calculated as the ratio of the crude prevalence in each comparison subgroup to that of the reference subgroup (women born before 1989, not eligible for rubella vaccination), with 95% CIs derived using the standard log-linear approximation and a continuity correction (+0.5) applied to comparisons involving zero-count cells.IgM seropositivity was interpreted descriptively as a possible marker of recent or acute rubella infection and was not used to estimate population-level rubella immunity; a positive IgM result alone does not equate to confirmed acute infection, since definitive confirmation would require IgG avidity testing or reverse-transcription PCR, both of which were outside the scope of this cross-sectional serological survey. 2.6.Vaccination eligibility cohortsParticipants were stratified into four subgroups based on year of birth as a proxy for eligibility for rubella vaccination in Romania, in accordance with the national immunization schedule (Table 1).Table 1Correspondence between birth year and eligibility for rubella vaccine in Romania.Birth year<198919891990199119921993199419951996…

title_original: Anti-Rubella antibodies seroprevalence among pregnant women in South-Western Romania

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to assess the seroprevalence of anti-rubella antibodies among pregnant women in South-Western Romania to evaluate immunity levels and identify potential gaps in vaccination coverage. This is important due to the risk of congenital rubella syndrome in fetuses if mothers are not immune during pregnancy.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This cross-sectional study was conducted in South-Western Romania between 2013 and 2022, focusing on pregnant women during their first trimester. Participants were stratified into four subgroups based on birth year, reflecting vaccination eligibility according to the national immunization schedule.
analysis.methods: Serological testing for anti-rubella IgM and IgG antibodies was performed using an electrochemiluminescence immunoassay (ECLIA) on the Cobas e601 analyzer. The study used prevalence ratios (PR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) to compare associations between vaccination eligibility cohorts and antibody seroprevalence, applying a continuity correction for zero-count cells.
analysis.main_results: The seroprevalence of acute rubella infection (IgM positive) was low and slightly decreased from 0.54% (2013–2016) to 0.50% (2019–2022). In rural areas, the highest seroprevalence was observed in women born between 1995 and 1996 (vaccination gap subgroup), while the lowest was in those born between 1989 and 1994 (eligible for RCV vaccine). The proportion of women tested in urban areas decreased significantly from Group 1 (223/367, 60.49%) to Group 2 (1,169/2,669, 43.80%; p < 0.001).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as indicating a slight decline in acute rubella infection rates, particularly in rural areas and among younger women, suggesting potential improvements in vaccination coverage. However, they emphasized that the wide confidence intervals for some comparisons indicate the need for further research to confirm these trends.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings provide insights into the current immunity status of pregnant women in South-Western Romania, which is crucial for informing targeted vaccination strategies and preventing congenital rubella syndrome. They also highlight the importance of addressing vaccination gaps in specific demographic subgroups.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's limitations include the use of a cross-sectional design, which precludes causal inferences, and the wide confidence intervals for some comparisons due to small sample sizes. The evidence is moderate in strength, as the results are based on serological data without definitive confirmation of acute infection through additional testing methods.

analysis.summary_en: This study assessed the seroprevalence of anti-rubella antibodies among pregnant women in South-Western Romania between 2013 and 2022. It found a slight decrease in acute rubella infection rates (IgM positive) from 0.54% to 0.50%, with the most notable decline in rural areas and among women aged 21–25 years. The study stratified participants into four subgroups based on birth year to reflect vaccination eligibility. While the overall IgG seroprevalence remained similar between the two periods, the proportion of women tested in urban areas decreased significantly. The authors interpreted these findings as suggesting potential improvements in vaccination coverage, though they cautioned that the wide confidence intervals for some comparisons indicate the need for further research. The study's cross-sectional design limits causal inferences, and the results are based on serological data without definitive confirmation of acute infection. These findings are relevant for informing targeted vaccination strategies and preventing congenital rubella syndrome, highlighting the importance of addressing vaccination gaps in specific demographic subgroups.

analysis_en.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to assess the seroprevalence of anti-rubella antibodies among pregnant women in South-Western Romania to evaluate immunity levels and identify potential gaps in vaccination coverage. This is important due to the risk of congenital rubella syndrome in fetuses if mothers are not immune during pregnancy.
analysis_en.study_design_and_population: This cross-sectional study was conducted in South-Western Romania between 2013 and 2022, focusing on pregnant women during their first trimester. Participants were stratified into four subgroups based on birth year, reflecting vaccination eligibility according to the national immunization schedule.
analysis_en.methods: Serological testing for anti-rubella IgM and IgG antibodies was performed using an electrochemiluminescence immunoassay (ECLIA) on the Cobas e601 analyzer. The study used prevalence ratios (PR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) to compare associations between vaccination eligibility cohorts and antibody seroprevalence, applying a continuity correction for zero-count cells.
analysis_en.main_results: The seroprevalence of acute rubella infection (IgM positive) was low and slightly decreased from 0.54% (2013–2016) to 0.50% (2019–2022). In rural areas, the highest seroprevalence was observed in women born between 1995 and 1996 (vaccination gap subgroup), while the lowest was in those born between 1989 and 1994 (eligible for RCV vaccine). The proportion of women tested in urban areas decreased significantly from Group 1 (223/367, 60.49%) to Group 2 (1,169/2,669, 43.80%; p < 0.001).
analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as indicating a slight decline in acute rubella infection rates, particularly in rural areas and among younger women, suggesting potential improvements in vaccination coverage. However, they emphasized that the wide confidence intervals for some comparisons indicate the need for further research to confirm these trends.
analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings provide insights into the current immunity status of pregnant women in South-Western Romania, which is crucial for informing targeted vaccination strategies and preventing congenital rubella syndrome. They also highlight the importance of addressing vaccination gaps in specific demographic subgroups.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's limitations include the use of a cross-sectional design, which precludes causal inferences, and the wide confidence intervals for some comparisons due to small sample sizes. The evidence is moderate in strength, as the results are based on serological data without definitive confirmation of acute infection through additional testing methods.

title: Determinants of childhood vaccination differ between conflict-affected and non-conflict regions in Cameroon

source_records.title: Determinants of childhood vaccination differ between conflict-affected and non-conflict regions in Cameroon

full_text: AbstractIntroductionChildhood vaccination remains one of the most effective public health interventions, yet coverage is often lowest in settings affected by conflict and structural disadvantage. Cameroon has faced overlapping humanitarian crises in its Far North, North-West, and South-West regions, but evidence comparing determinants of full vaccination between conflict-affected and non-conflict regions remains limited. This study explores determinants of full vaccination status in 12–23 months children in Cameroon, stratified by conflict regions.MethodsWe conducted a secondary analysis of the 2018 Cameroon Demographic and Health Survey, including 1,824 living children aged 12–23 months. Full basic vaccination was defined as receipt of one dose of BCG, three doses of pentavalent vaccine, three doses of polio vaccine, and one dose of measles vaccine. Survey-weighted logistic regression was used to identify factors associated with full vaccination overall and by conflict status.ResultsOverall, 53.08% of children were fully vaccinated. Coverage was lower in conflict-affected than in non-conflict regions (45.29% versus 55.97%). In unadjusted analysis, conflict status was associated with lower odds of full vaccination, but this association was no longer significant in the adjusted model. At the national level, higher odds of full vaccination were associated with richer household wealth, maternal secondary or higher education, antenatal care attendance, and postnatal care. In conflict-affected regions, maternal secondary or higher education, postnatal care, and facility delivery remained significant predictors of full vaccination.DiscussionFull vaccination coverage in Cameroon remains below desirable levels, with lower crude coverage in conflict-affected regions. However, after adjustment, conflict status was not independently associated with full vaccination, suggesting that socioeconomic conditions and contact with maternal health services are more important determinants. Strengthening antenatal and postnatal care and reducing socioeconomic barriers may improve vaccination coverage, especially in fragile settings.Keywords: Cameroon, conflict-affected settings, Demographic and Health Survey, health inequalities, immunization, vaccination coverage Materials and methodsEthics statementThe Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) of Cameroon conducted between June 2018 and January 2019 (EDSC-V) by the National Institute of Statistics, in close collaboration with the Ministry of Public Health (24). The DHS protocol was reviewed and approved by the ICF Institutional Review Board - ICF IRB FWA00000845 - and by the Cameroon National Ethics Committee for Human Health (CNERSH) -132989.0.000. CM. DHS.01. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to data collection. The datasets used in this study are publicly available and anonymized, and therefore no additional ethical approval was required for this secondary analysis (ICRC Ethics Process exemption reference GVA_CORE_1925). The DHS and ICF granted access to the dataset on the 14 August 2025.MaterialsThe analysis was conducted using data from the 2018 Cameroon Demographic and Health Survey (DHS). The DHS uses a two-stage stratified cluster sampling design to obtain a nationally representative sample of households. In the first stage, clusters (enumeration areas) were selected from the national sampling frame with probability proportional to size. In the second stage, households were randomly selected within each cluster. The survey collected detailed information on maternal and child health, including vaccination history for children born in the five years preceding the survey. This study used the Children’s Recode (KR) dataset. The analysis was restricted to living children, one per household, aged 12–23 months at the time of the survey, which is the standard age group used to assess completion of basic childhood vaccination. The analysis was restricted to children aged 12–23 months because, according to the national immunization schedule, all vaccines included in the definition of full vaccination should have been administered by 12 months of age. Children with missing information on vaccination status were excluded from the corresponding analyses.MethodsThe outcome variable was full basic vaccination status. A child was considered fully vaccinated if they had received one dose of Bacille Calmette–Guérin (BCG), three doses of pentavalent vaccine, three doses of polio vaccine (excluding the birth dose), and one dose of measles vaccine. Vaccination was considered received if the vaccination date was recorded on the card, the vaccination was marked on the card without a date, or the mother reported that the child had received the vaccine.The main exposure of interest was residence in a conflict-affected region. The Far North, North-West, and South-West regions were classified as conflict-affected because they have experienced sustained armed conflict during the study period, whereas the remaining seven regions were classified as non-conflict regions. This classification was based on the regional level available in the DHS dataset, which represents the finest geographic resolution accessible for public-use data. All other regions were classified as non-conflict regions. Figure 1 shows the geographical classification of conflict-affected and non-conflict regions of Cameroon. The 2018 DHS was conducted during ongoing armed conflict, and the DHS final report notes that insecurity prevented complete coverage of some areas of the South-West region, resulting in partial under-representation of that region.Figure 1Classification of the ten administrative regions of Cameroon into conflict-affected (Far North, North-West, and South-West) and non-conflict regions used for the analyses.Map of Cameroon showing conflict-affected regions in dark brown and non-conflict regions in light peach, with two regions in the north and north-west marked as conflict-affected according to the legend.Potential determinants of full vaccination included child, maternal, household, and health service utilization characteristics, as suggested in previous literature (25). These variables included sex of the child, parity (categorized into two groups using the sample median to provide a simple comparison between women with lower and higher parity and to maintain comparability between groups), maternal age group (15–24, 25–34, and 35–49 years), maternal education (no education, primary, secondary or higher), household wealth quintile (Poorest, Poorer, Middle, Richer or Richest), place of residence (urban or rural), perceived distance to a health facility (big problem vs. not a big problem), number of antenatal care visits during pregnancy (0, 1–3, ≥4 visits), place of delivery (home vs. health facility), and postnatal care for the newborn.Statistical analysisDescriptive statistics were calculated to summarize the characteristics of the study population. Weighted percentages were reported together with unweighted frequencies. Differences between conflict-affected and non-conflict regions were assessed using design-adjusted Pearson chi-square tests. Associations between explanatory variables and full vaccination were examined using survey-weighted logistic regression models, and statistical significance was evaluated using Wald tests. All analyses accounted for the complex sampling design of the DHS by applying sampling weights and adjusting for clustering at the primary sampling unit level and stratification. Potential interaction effects between selected covariates, including conflict status with maternal education, household wealth, and antenatal care visits, were explored by including multiplicative interaction terms in the survey-weighted logistic regression models. Interaction terms with p < 0.05 were considered statistically significant and retained in the final model. As none of the interaction terms reached statistical significance, they were not retained in the final models. Model discrimination was assessed using Tjur’s coefficient of discrimination (Tjur’s R2), calculated as the difference between the mean predicted probabilities among fully vaccinated and non-fully vaccinated children. Observations with missing values in variables included in the regression analyses were excluded using complete-case analysis. Missing data were minimal for all study variables, with the exception of antenatal care visits, for which 119 observations (6.5%) had missing information. Bivariate logistic regression analyses were performed to examine the association between each independent variable and full vaccination status. Candidate explanatory variables were selected a priori based on previous literature and their potential relevance to childhood vaccination. Among these candidate variables, those associated with the outcome at p < 0.20 in bivariable analyses were entered into the multivariable logistic regression models. The p < 0.20 threshold was chosen to avoid excluding potentially important confounders during model building (26, 27). Separate multivariable models were estimated for the entire country, for conflict-affected regions, and for non-conflict regions. Multicollinearity among the explanatory variables was assessed using variance inflation factors (VIFs). No evidence of problematic multicollinearity was observed for the three models. Adjusted odds ratios (AORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were reported. Statistical significance in the final models was defined as a two-sided p-value <0.05.All statistical analyses were performed using Stata (version 16; StataCorp, College Station, TX, USA). full_text_sections.methods: Materials and methodsEthics statementThe Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) of Cameroon conducted between June 2018 and January 2019 (EDSC-V) by the National Institute of Statistics, in close collaboration with the Ministry of Public Health (24). The DHS protocol was reviewed and approved by the ICF Institutional Review Board - ICF IRB FWA00000845 - and by the Cameroon National Ethics Committee for Human Health (CNERSH) -132989.0.000. CM. DHS.01. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to data collection. The datasets used in this study are publicly available and anonymized, and therefore no additional ethical approval was required for this secondary analysis (ICRC Ethics Process exemption reference GVA_CORE_1925). The DHS and ICF granted access to the dataset on the 14 August 2025.MaterialsThe analysis was conducted using data from the 2018 Cameroon Demographic and Health Survey (DHS). The DHS uses a two-stage stratified cluster sampling design to obtain a nationally representative sample of households. In the first stage, clusters (enumeration areas) were selected from the national sampling frame with probability proportional to size. In the second stage, households were randomly selected within each cluster. The survey collected detailed information on maternal and child health, including vaccination history for children born in the five years preceding the survey. This study used the Children’s Recode (KR) dataset. The analysis was restricted to living children, one per household, aged 12–23 months at the time of the survey, which is the standard age group used to assess completion of basic childhood vaccination. The analysis was restricted to children aged 12–23 months because, according to the national immunization schedule, all vaccines included in the definition of full vaccination should have been administered by 12 months of age. Children with missing information on vaccination status were excluded from the corresponding analyses.MethodsThe outcome variable was full basic vaccination status. A child was considered fully vaccinated if they had received one dose of Bacille Calmette–Guérin (BCG), three doses of pentavalent vaccine, three doses of polio vaccine (excluding the birth dose), and one dose of measles vaccine. Vaccination was considered received if the vaccination date was recorded on the card, the vaccination was marked on the card without a date, or the mother reported that the child had received the vaccine.The main exposure of interest was residence in a conflict-affected region. The Far North, North-West, and South-West regions were classified as conflict-affected because they have experienced sustained armed conflict during the study period, whereas the remaining seven regions were classified as non-conflict regions. This classification was based on the regional level available in the DHS dataset, which represents the finest geographic resolution accessible for public-use data. All other regions were classified as non-conflict regions. Figure 1 shows the geographical classification of conflict-affected and non-conflict regions of Cameroon. The 2018 DHS was conducted during ongoing armed conflict, and the DHS final report notes that insecurity prevented complete coverage of some areas of the South-West region, resulting in partial under-representation of that region.Figure 1Classification of the ten administrative regions of Cameroon into conflict-affected (Far North, North-West, and South-West) and non-conflict regions used for the analyses.Map of Cameroon showing conflict-affected regions in dark brown and non-conflict regions in light peach, with two regions in the north and north-west marked as conflict-affected according to the legend.Potential determinants of full vaccination included child, maternal, household, and health service utilization characteristics, as suggested in previous literature (25). These variables included sex of the child, parity (categorized into two groups using the sample median to provide a simple comparison between women with lower and higher parity and to maintain comparability between groups), maternal age group (15–24, 25–34, and 35–49 years), maternal education (no education, primary, secondary or higher), household wealth quintile (Poorest, Poorer, Middle, Richer or Richest), place of residence (urban or rural), perceived distance to a health facility (big problem vs. not a big problem), number of antenatal care visits during pregnancy (0, 1–3, ≥4 visits), place of delivery (home vs. health facility), and postnatal care for the newborn.Statistical analysisDescriptive statistics were calculated to summarize the characteristics of the study population. Weighted percentages were reported together with unweighted frequencies. Differences between conflict-affected and non-conflict regions were assessed using design-adjusted Pearson chi-square tests. Associations between explanatory variables and full vaccination were examined using survey-weighted logistic regression models, and statistical significance was evaluated using Wald tests. All analyses accounted for the complex sampling design of the DHS by applying sampling weights and adjusting for clustering at the primary sampling unit level and stratification. Potential interaction effects between selected covariates, including conflict status with maternal education, household wealth, and antenatal care visits, were explored by including multiplicative interaction terms in the survey-weighted logistic regression models. Interaction terms with p < 0.05 were considered statistically significant and retained in the final model. As none of the interaction terms reached statistical significance, they were not retained in the final models. Model discrimination was assessed using Tjur’s coefficient of discrimination (Tjur’s R2), calculated as the difference between the mean predicted probabilities among fully vaccinated and non-fully vaccinated children. Observations with missing values in variables included in the regression analyses were excluded using complete-case analysis. Missing data were minimal for all study variables, with the exception of antenatal care visits, for which 119 observations (6.5%) had missing information. Bivariate logistic regression analyses were performed to examine the association between each independent variable and full vaccination status. Candidate explanatory variables were selected a priori based on previous literature and their potential relevance to childhood vaccination. Among these candidate variables, those associated with the outcome at p < 0.20 in bivariable analyses were entered into the multivariable logistic regression models. The p < 0.20 threshold was chosen to avoid excluding potentially important confounders during model building (26, 27). Separate multivariable models were estimated for the entire country, for conflict-affected regions, and for non-conflict regions. Multicollinearity among the explanatory variables was assessed using variance inflation factors (VIFs). No evidence of problematic multicollinearity was observed for the three models. Adjusted odds ratios (AORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were reported. Statistical significance in the final models was defined as a two-sided p-value <0.05.All statistical analyses were performed using Stata (version 16; StataCorp, College Station, TX, USA). full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionSummary of main findingsThis study examined the determinants of full basic childhood vaccination among children aged 12–23 months in Cameroon using nationally representative data from the 2018 Demographic and Health Survey. Overall, just over half of children were fully vaccinated, and vaccination coverage was consistently lower in conflict-affected regions compared with non-conflict regions. In the national model, full vaccination was significantly associated with household wealth, maternal education, antenatal care attendance, and postnatal care for the newborn. An important finding of this study is that, although children living in conflict-affected regions had lower crude vaccination coverage than those living in non-conflict regions, conflict status itself was not independently associated with full vaccination after adjustment. This suggests that the observed disparity in vaccination coverage may be largely explained by differences in socioeconomic conditions and access to maternal and child health services rather than conflict exposure alone. These findings highlight the importance of addressing the underlying structural barriers to immunization in conflict-affected settings, while recognizing that conflict may still indirectly influence vaccination through its effects on healthcare delivery and household vulnerability.Differences between conflict and non-conflict regionsThis study also provides important insights into how determinants of vaccination differ between conflict-affected and non-conflict regions. Children living in conflict-affected regions had lower vaccination coverage overall, which is consistent with previous evidence showing that armed conflict can disrupt health systems, reduce access to services, and undermine routine immunization programs (9, 12). In addition, attacks against healthcare workers, vaccinators and health facilities, as well as insecurity limiting the movement of healthcare personnel, may further disrupt routine immunization activities and reduce access to vaccination services in conflict-affected settings (28, 29). Our findings are also consistent with reports from Cameroon documenting reductions in routine immunization coverage during periods of insecurity, particularly in the South-West region, where armed conflict has challenged the delivery of vaccination services and supplementary immunization activities (20–22, 30). Conflict status was no longer independently associated with full vaccination after adjustment for socioeconomic and healthcare-related factors. However, this finding should not be interpreted as evidence that conflict has no influence on childhood immunization. Rather, it suggests that the crude association was largely explained by differences in socioeconomic characteristics and access to maternal healthcare services, which may themselves represent pathways through which conflict influences childhood vaccination. This interpretation is consistent with the broader literature showing that armed conflict affects immunization primarily through disruption of health services, displacement, reduced access to care, and deterioration of socioeconomic conditions (9, 12). One possible explanation is that the extensive humanitarian response implemented in conflict-affected regions, in collaboration with local health authorities, may have mitigated some of the adverse effects of conflict on routine immunization services (30–32). However, this hypothesis could not be directly evaluated using the available DHS data and should therefore be interpreted with caution.In conflict settings, maternal education and healthcare contact points such as postnatal care and facility delivery appeared particularly important for vaccination uptake. These factors may serve as critical entry points for maintaining vaccination coverage in contexts where health systems are weakened and access to routine services is limited. In contrast, in non-conflict regions socioeconomic inequalities and maternal health service utilization remained the dominant determinants of vaccination. This suggests that while the structural determinants of vaccination remain broadly similar across settings, the relative importance of specific factors may differ depending on the context. This pattern is also consistent with observations from other conflict-affected African settings, including Northeast Nigeria, where caregivers identified disruption of health services, insecurity, and continued engagement with healthcare providers as key factors influencing childhood vaccination uptake (11, 12).Socioeconomic inequalities in vaccination coverageOur findings highlight the important role of socioeconomic factors in determining childhood vaccination coverage. Children from wealthier households had significantly higher odds of being fully vaccinated compared with those from poorer households, particularly in non-conflict regions. These findings are also in agreement with a recent DHS-based analysis from Cameroon, which identified maternal education and healthcare utilization as major determinants of childhood vaccination, although that study focused on pentavalent vaccine uptake rather than complete basic vaccination and did not specifically examine differences between conflict-affected and non-conflict regions (23). Similar socioeconomic gradients in vaccination coverage have been documented in many low- and middle-income countries, where economic resources influence access to health services, transportation, and information about preventive care (33, 34).Maternal education also emerged as an important determinant of vaccination. Children whose mothers had secondary or higher education were significantly more likely to be fully vaccinated, especially in conflict-affected regions. Educated mothers may have greater awareness of the benefits of immunization, better understanding of vaccination schedules, and increased ability to navigate health systems. Previous studies using DHS data from sub-Saharan Africa have consistently reported positive associations between maternal education and childhood vaccination uptake (33–35).Importance of health service utilizationUtilization of maternal health services was strongly associated with vaccination completion. Antenatal care attendance was one of the strongest predictors of full vaccination in both the national and non-conflict models. Mothers who attended antenatal care visits were substantially more likely to have children who completed the basic vaccination schedule. Antenatal care provides important opportunities for health education and counseling, including information about the importance of childhood immunization and the recommended vaccination schedule. Antenatal care attendance has also been proved to increase the likelihood of other mother–child health outcomes, such as delivery in health facility and start breastfeeding of the baby (36, 37).Postnatal care for the newborn was also significantly associated with vaccination completion in all models. Postnatal visits represent critical contact points between families and the health system, during which healthcare providers can reinforce immunization messages, verify vaccination status, and facilitate timely follow-up vaccinations. The lower availability of vaccination cards observed in conflict-affected regions may also reflect broader disruptions in continuity of healthcare. Insecurity, population displacement, and interruptions in routine health services may compromise the retention of personal health records, making it more difficult for caregivers and healthcare providers to verify previous vaccinations and ensure timely completion of the recommended immunization schedule.In conflict-affected regions, facility-based delivery was an additional determinant of full vaccination. Health facility delivery may facilitate early contact with vaccination services, including administration of birth-dose vaccines and registration into routine immunization…
full_text_sections.conclusion: ConclusionIn conclusion, full basic childhood vaccination coverage in Cameroon remains suboptimal and is lower in conflict-affected regions. Socioeconomic factors and utilization of maternal health services are key determinants of vaccination completion. Strengthening antenatal and postnatal care services and addressing socioeconomic barriers may improve vaccination coverage, particularly in conflict-affected areas.
full_text_sections.other: IntroductionDisease prevention through childhood vaccination has been proved to be one of the most effective interventions that saved, and continue to save, million lives worldwide: it is estimated that every year vaccination can avert approximately two million deaths; moreover, vaccination reduces childhood morbidity and disability. Since 1974, when the Expanded Programme of Immunization was launched, it is estimated that vaccination has prevented 146 million deaths among children under 5 years of age (1–3).Sustained high immunization coverage is essential to maximize the impact of vaccination programs and to protect individuals who cannot be vaccinated. This protection relies on herd immunity, which occurs when a sufficiently large proportion of the population is immune to interrupt pathogen transmission. For highly transmissible diseases such as measles, vaccination coverage of around 95% is generally required to prevent outbreaks. Failure to achieve and maintain such coverage increases the risk of outbreaks, particularly in settings where immunization services are disrupted (4–7).Maintaining sufficient vaccination coverage to achieve herd immunity thresholds faces multiple challenges. Concurrent pandemics, public health emergencies, population movements, vaccine hesitancy, and misinformation can all disrupt immunization efforts (8–11). Countries affected by armed conflict typically exhibit lower vaccination coverage, higher incidence and mortality from vaccine-preventable diseases, and elevated risk of epidemics (12). These patterns underscore the compounded risks in settings like Cameroon, where ongoing crises in the Far North, North-West, and South-West regions further constrain immunization programmes. In this context, understanding the current level of vaccination coverage is essential. Vaccination coverage among children in Cameroon is still lower than the target set globally: in 2018, national coverage with the first dose of measles-containing vaccine in Cameroon was approximately 61%, well below the ≥95% coverage generally required to prevent measles outbreaks and below the Immunization Agenda 2030 target of at least 90% national coverage (13, 14).Cameroon is a lower-middle-income country in Central Africa with a population of approximately 28 million people. It is characterized by considerable linguistic, ethnic, and religious diversity, with French and English as its official languages. Despite its natural resources, poverty remains widespread, with approximately 40% of the population living below the national poverty line, and persistent socioeconomic inequalities and ongoing armed conflicts continue to challenge equitable access to healthcare, including childhood immunization (15). Cameroon has experienced overlapping humanitarian crises in its Far North, North-West, and South-West regions over the past decade. In the Far North, armed violence linked to Boko Haram and affiliated groups emerged around 2014, causing recurrent attacks on civilians, population displacement, and a sustained security response by national and regional forces. In the predominantly Anglophone North-West and South-West regions—where approximately 20% of the population resides—protests by lawyers, teachers, and other professional groups began in late 2016 over concerns including language use in courts and schools, perceived marginalization, and central governance structures; these escalated from 2017 into armed confrontation between state security forces and non-state armed groups. These situations have led to substantial internal displacement, restricted access to services, and humanitarian needs across affected areas, with hundreds of thousands of people reported as internally displaced persons and millions requiring assistance (16–19).Very few studies have been conducted to assess the vaccination coverage and its predictors in Cameroon. Although these studies are methodologically robust and valid, they focused on limited factors, such as the dropout in coverage due to the COVID19 pandemic (20, 21), are limited in terms of geographical areas and sample size (22) or focused on the coverage of a specific antigen (23). However, these studies agree on the fact that childhood vaccination coverage in the Cameroon is low and subjected to decline in case of other emergencies. On the other hand, these studies do not systematically assess various levels of factors associated with childhood vaccination in the country, nor compare regions affected by armed conflict with more stable areas.The aim of this study is to explore factors associated with childhood vaccination coverage in Cameroon using the most recent countrywide vaccination coverage survey (DHS 2018); to compare such factors between regions affected by armed conflict with regions more stable; to propose strategies to increase vaccination coverage overall and for specific subgroups of populations. analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate how determinants of childhood vaccination differ between conflict-affected and non-conflict regions in Cameroon, addressing a public health problem related to vaccine coverage in unstable settings.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A cross-sectional analysis using data from the 2018 Cameroon Demographic and Health Survey was conducted on 1,824 children aged 12–23 months, with the study restricted to those who had all vaccines included in the definition of full vaccination by 12 months of age.
analysis.methods: Survey-weighted logistic regression models were used to assess associations between explanatory variables and full vaccination status, with statistical significance evaluated using Wald tests. Design-adjusted Pearson chi-square tests were used to compare differences between conflict-affected and non-conflict regions. Interaction effects were explored by including multiplicative terms in the regression models.
analysis.main_results: Overall, 53.08% of children were fully vaccinated. In unadjusted analysis, conflict status was associated with lower odds of full vaccination, but this association was no longer significant in the adjusted model. Rural residence was more common in conflict-affected regions (74.55%) than in non-conflict regions (50.17%).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that conflict status alone was not a significant determinant of vaccination completion after adjusting for other factors, highlighting the importance of socioeconomic and healthcare access variables in influencing vaccination rates.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform public health strategies by emphasizing the need to address socioeconomic disparities and improve healthcare access in conflict-affected regions to enhance vaccination coverage.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study was limited by potential under-representation of conflict-affected areas due to insecurity, and missing data on antenatal care visits. Despite these limitations, the evidence is moderate due to the use of survey-weighted methods and adjustment for complex sampling design.

analysis.summary_en: This study examines the determinants of childhood vaccination in Cameroon, comparing conflict-affected and non-conflict regions. It highlights that while conflict status initially appeared to be associated with lower vaccination rates, this association disappeared after adjusting for socioeconomic and healthcare access factors. The research underscores the importance of addressing disparities in wealth, education, and healthcare utilization to improve vaccination coverage. The study used data from the 2018 Cameroon Demographic and Health Survey, applying survey-weighted logistic regression and chi-square tests to account for sampling complexities. Limitations include potential under-representation of conflict-affected areas and missing data, which may affect the generalizability of the findings. The results suggest that targeted interventions should focus on improving access to healthcare services and addressing socioeconomic barriers in conflict-affected regions to enhance vaccination rates.

elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究的局限性在于,由于不安全因素,受冲突影响地区的代表性可能不足,而且产前保健就诊数据缺失。尽管存在这些局限性,但由于使用了调查加权方法和对复杂抽样设计进行了调整,证据仍然有限。

This study used the Children’s Recode (KR) dataset. title: Editorial: Mathematical Modelling and data analysis in infectious diseases

full_text: SummaryThis Research Topic brings together 22 contributions that showcase the breadth of mathematical and computational tools now used to understand and respond to infectious disease threats. Spanning mechanistic modeling, statistical forecasting, machine learning, stochastic optimization, computational fluid dynamics, and burden analysis, the Research Topic addresses diseases ranging from COVID-19 and influenza to measles, mumps, and dengue. Contributions cluster around three central themes: extracting robust, decision-relevant forecasts from noisy real-time surveillance data; modeling how interventions, mobility, and connectivity shape transmission dynamics; and linking disease burden to environmental, socioeconomic, and health-system determinants. Together, these papers reinforce a unifying message: no single method suffices for every question, and the right analytical approach must be matched to the decision at hand, the data-generating process, and the practical consequences of getting the inference wrong. IntroductionInfectious diseases spread through a complex mix of factors, including pathogens, hosts, behavior, mobility, environment, health systems, and interventions, all of which interact with each other. Mathematical models and data analysis are essential tools for understanding and scientifically simulating these interactions. These approaches enable researchers to draw robust conclusions from incomplete data, formalize competing hypotheses regarding pathogen transmissions and intervention effects, and integrate diverse sources of evidence to generate forecasts and support evidence-based decision-making. The coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic accelerated the use of these tools on an unprecedented scale, with mathematical models informing decisions regarding lockdowns, vaccine allocations, and healthcare capacity-based planning in near real time. But the pandemic also made clear that good models need clear and evidence-based assumptions, must be tested against real data, should be checked against new data whenever possible, and must be used with an understanding of their uncertainty, not treated as perfect predictions (1–3). The challenge has only grown since: infectious-disease data are increasingly high-dimensional and multimodal, spanning genomic surveillance, mobility traces, wastewater signals, and electronic health records, while the methodological toolkit available to analyze them has expanded just as quickly, from classical compartmental models to machine learning and stochastic optimization.The Research Topic Mathematical Modeling and data analysis in infectious diseases responds to this landscape by bringing together 22 contributions spanning public health, applied mathematics, infectious-disease epidemiology, and microbial sciences. The Research Topic covers a wide range of approaches, such as mechanistic modeling, statistical forecasting, machine learning, stochastic optimization, computational fluid dynamics, and burden analyses, applied across diseases including COVID-19, influenza, measles, mumps, dengue, and other pathogens of public health concern. Its unifying message is simple: no single method suffices for every question. Instead, the choice of method should follow from the decision at hand, the process generating the data, the observations actually available, and the consequences of incorrect inference or prediction. Robust inference and disease forecastingSeveral contributions in this Research Topic address a central challenge in infectious-disease surveillance: extracting stable, decision-relevant predictions from data that evolve in real time. Rojas-Díaz et al. propose a robust calibration framework for delayed compartmental models, employing controlled parameter initialization and time-varying parameters to fit COVID-19 incidence, intensive-care burden, and effective reproduction numbers across Chilean regions. Their work underscores practical identifiability and numerical stability as prerequisites for translating mechanistic models into tools that can be used operationally in public health decision-making.A complementary forecasting stream combines classical time-series methods with nonlinear learning. Xian et al. demonstrate that a SARIMA–k-nearest-neighbor (SARIMA-KNN) hybrid model improves prediction of acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis in Chongqing, China, relative to its component models and Prophet-based comparators. Cao et al. integrated ARIMA and bidirectional long short-term memory networks through genetic-algorithm weighting, reporting improved COVID-19 forecasts for Japan with external validation in Germany. Alahmadi et al. applied seasonal-trend decomposition together with LightGBM to forecast post-pandemic influenza A in Saudi Arabia, illustrating the value of hybrid approaches when seasonal patterns are disrupted by structural change. Collectively, these studies point to an important direction for surveillance practice: hybrid models can disentangle recurrent linear or seasonal structure from irregular non-linear behavior, but their value depends on prospective evaluation and reporting forecasts alongside calibrated measures of uncertainty (3, 4).The Research Topic also moves beyond single-location time series. One contribution introduces a spatiotemporal graph-learning framework that leverages geographic and origin-destination relationships to capture both contemporaneous neighborhood effects and lagged spatial spillovers in infectious-disease prediction (Liu et al.). Taken together with the forecasting studies above, this work underscores that local incidence is shaped not only by its own history but also by connections to other places, reporting processes, and shifting epidemic regimes. Beyond spatial and temporal structure, several contributions strengthen the statistical foundations needed for infectious-disease data that are non-normal, highly skewed, or operationally heterogeneous. Gharaibeh et al. introduced a two-parameter skewed Loai distribution for positive, right-skewed data and demonstrate its competitive fit to COVID-19 mortality data. At the healthcare-facility scale, Chen and Zhou compared SARIMA, ETS, Prophet, and NNETAR models for forecasting multidrug-resistant organism infection rates, showing that model choice should reflect both forecast accuracy and residual diagnostics rather than point-error measures alone. Disease transmission, interventions, and mobilityMechanistic models offer a principled way to represent intervention timing, human behavior, and disease progression explicitly within the model structure. Babasola et al. formulated a time-delayed model for a potential human outbreak of highly pathogenic avian influenza, explicitly incorporating incubation, vaccine deployment, vaccine-to-protection delays, vaccine acceptance, residual susceptibility, and compliance with non-pharmaceutical interventions. Their simulations illustrate why early deployment and rapid protection are critical, and why non-pharmaceutical interventions remain especially important before vaccine-induced protection takes effect. Building on this theme, Ntaimo et al. developed an integrated chance-constrained stochastic-programming model for optimal COVID-19 vaccination and intervention strategies across multiple municipalities in Gauteng, South Africa. By incorporating uncertainty in contact patterns, household transmission, age-specific susceptibility and infectivity, and multiple vaccine-effectiveness endpoints, their approach makes risk tolerance an explicit part of allocation decisions. This work exemplifies a valuable bridge between epidemic modeling and operations research: the goal is not merely to simulate an outbreak but also to identify feasible actions under uncertainty.Mobility is another recurring mechanism in this Research Topic. Drawing on cases from 294 Chinese cities, high-speed-rail records, migration data, and socioeconomic covariates, Zhang et al. found that rail connectivity was associated with early intercity dissemination of COVID-19 and that the Wuhan lockdown and transport suspensions disrupted this pathway. The importance of connectivity is echoed in a different setting: an age-structured, stochastic model of measles outbreaks in Northern British Columbia. Irvine et al. showed that inter-community mobility and school-based contact can increase outbreak probability and diminish the effectiveness of interventions, while the combined use of post-exposure prophylaxis and active case finding substantially reduces outbreak risk across scenarios.At a finer spatial scale, Chong et al. combined epidemiological analyses of high-rise residences in Singapore with computational fluid-dynamics simulations, identifying elevated risk within vertical building stacks, and showed how wind direction and cross-ventilation can shape plausible aerosol transport pathways. Together, these contributions demonstrate that interventions must be conditioned on the structure of connectivity itself: rail networks, buildings, households, and social contacts each create distinct transmission pathways that call for correspondingly tailored control measures. He et al. assessed meteorological influences on influenza incidence in Wuxi, while Yao et al. examined environmental determinants of influenza-like illness across cities in Fujian Province between 2015 and 2023. Tao et al. characterized severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome and its meteorological associations in Jiangsu Province. Extending this line of work, Guo et al. applied generalized additive and distributed lag non-linear models to identify non-linear, interacting, and delayed meteorological associations with hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome on China's Jiaodong Peninsula. Hao and Yu take a broader ecological view, using provincial panel models to examine bacillary dysentery in China and link incidence to healthcare capacity, economic development, and forest coverage. full_text_sections.other: IntroductionInfectious diseases spread through a complex mix of factors, including pathogens, hosts, behavior, mobility, environment, health systems, and interventions, all of which interact with each other. Mathematical models and data analysis are essential tools for understanding and scientifically simulating these interactions. These approaches enable researchers to draw robust conclusions from incomplete data, formalize competing hypotheses regarding pathogen transmissions and intervention effects, and integrate diverse sources of evidence to generate forecasts and support evidence-based decision-making. The coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic accelerated the use of these tools on an unprecedented scale, with mathematical models informing decisions regarding lockdowns, vaccine allocations, and healthcare capacity-based planning in near real time. But the pandemic also made clear that good models need clear and evidence-based assumptions, must be tested against real data, should be checked against new data whenever possible, and must be used with an understanding of their uncertainty, not treated as perfect predictions (1–3). The challenge has only grown since: infectious-disease data are increasingly high-dimensional and multimodal, spanning genomic surveillance, mobility traces, wastewater signals, and electronic health records, while the methodological toolkit available to analyze them has expanded just as quickly, from classical compartmental models to machine learning and stochastic optimization.The Research Topic Mathematical Modeling and data analysis in infectious diseases responds to this landscape by bringing together 22 contributions spanning public health, applied mathematics, infectious-disease epidemiology, and microbial sciences. The Research Topic covers a wide range of approaches, such as mechanistic modeling, statistical forecasting, machine learning, stochastic optimization, computational fluid dynamics, and burden analyses, applied across diseases including COVID-19, influenza, measles, mumps, dengue, and other pathogens of public health concern. Its unifying message is simple: no single method suffices for every question. Instead, the choice of method should follow from the decision at hand, the process generating the data, the observations actually available, and the consequences of incorrect inference or prediction. Robust inference and disease forecastingSeveral contributions in this Research Topic address a central challenge in infectious-disease surveillance: extracting stable, decision-relevant predictions from data that evolve in real time. Rojas-Díaz et al. propose a robust calibration framework for delayed compartmental models, employing controlled parameter initialization and time-varying parameters to fit COVID-19 incidence, intensive-care burden, and effective reproduction numbers across Chilean regions. Their work underscores practical identifiability and numerical stability as prerequisites for translating mechanistic models into tools that can be used operationally in public health decision-making.A complementary forecasting stream combines classical time-series methods with nonlinear learning. Xian et al. demonstrate that a SARIMA–k-nearest-neighbor (SARIMA-KNN) hybrid model improves prediction of acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis in Chongqing, China, relative to its component models and Prophet-based comparators. Cao et al. integrated ARIMA and bidirectional long short-term memory networks through genetic-algorithm weighting, reporting improved COVID-19 forecasts for Japan with external validation in Germany. Alahmadi et al. applied seasonal-trend decomposition together with LightGBM to forecast post-pandemic influenza A in Saudi Arabia, illustrating the value of hybrid approaches when seasonal patterns are disrupted by structural change. Collectively, these studies point to an important direction for surveillance practice: hybrid models can disentangle recurrent linear or seasonal structure from irregular non-linear behavior, but their value depends on prospective evaluation and reporting forecasts alongside calibrated measures of uncertainty (3, 4).The Research Topic also moves beyond single-location time series. One contribution introduces a spatiotemporal graph-learning framework that leverages geographic and origin-destination relationships to capture both contemporaneous neighborhood effects and lagged spatial spillovers in infectious-disease prediction (Liu et al.). Taken together with the forecasting studies above, this work underscores that local incidence is shaped not only by its own history but also by connections to other places, reporting processes, and shifting epidemic regimes. Beyond spatial and temporal structure, several contributions strengthen the statistical foundations needed for infectious-disease data that are non-normal, highly skewed, or operationally heterogeneous. Gharaibeh et al. introduced a two-parameter skewed Loai distribution for positive, right-skewed data and demonstrate its competitive fit to COVID-19 mortality data. At the healthcare-facility scale, Chen and Zhou compared SARIMA, ETS, Prophet, and NNETAR models for forecasting multidrug-resistant organism infection rates, showing that model choice should reflect both forecast accuracy and residual diagnostics rather than point-error measures alone. Babasola et al. formulated a time-delayed model for a potential human outbreak of highly pathogenic avian influenza, explicitly incorporating incubation, vaccine deployment, vaccine-to-protection delays, vaccine acceptance, residual susceptibility, and compliance with non-pharmaceutical interventions. Their simulations illustrate why early deployment and rapid protection are critical, and why non-pharmaceutical interventions remain especially important before vaccine-induced protection takes effect. Building on this theme, Ntaimo et al. developed an integrated chance-constrained stochastic-programming model for optimal COVID-19 vaccination and intervention strategies across multiple municipalities in Gauteng, South Africa. analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addresses the challenge of extracting stable, decision-relevant predictions from real-time infectious-disease data, which is essential for effective public health surveillance and response.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The Research Topic includes 22 contributions from public health, applied mathematics, infectious-disease epidemiology, and microbial sciences, covering diseases such as measles, influenza, dengue, and others of public health concern.
analysis.methods: The Research Topic spans mechanistic modeling, statistical forecasting, machine learning, stochastic optimization, computational fluid dynamics, and burden analysis, with a focus on integrating these methods across diverse diseases and contexts.
analysis.main_results: The studies show that contextual covariates can strengthen local early warning and risk stratification when non-linear and place-specific effects are properly accounted for, and that rail connectivity was associated with early intercity dissemination of COVID-19.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that interventions must be tailored to the structure of connectivity, such as rail networks, buildings, and social contacts, which create distinct transmission pathways. This highlights the need for context-sensitive modeling and analysis.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform the development of more accurate surveillance tools and highlight the importance of integrating environmental, socioeconomic, and health-system data to improve public health decision-making.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is moderate, as it is based on a collection of studies rather than a single, focused experiment, and the generalizability of results depends on the specific context and data sources used.

analysis.summary_en: This editorial discusses the growing importance of mathematical modeling and data analysis in infectious disease research, particularly in the context of real-time surveillance and forecasting. The Research Topic includes 22 contributions from various disciplines, addressing diseases such as measles, influenza, and dengue. It highlights the use of diverse methods, including mechanistic modeling, statistical forecasting, and machine learning, to understand disease transmission dynamics and improve public health responses. The studies show that contextual factors, such as rail connectivity and environmental conditions, play a significant role in disease spread and that interventions must be tailored to specific transmission pathways. These findings emphasize the need for robust statistical foundations and context-sensitive interpretation in infectious disease modeling. However, the evidence is moderate due to the collection nature of the studies and the reliance on diverse data sources, which may affect generalizability.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究解决了从实时传染病数据中提取稳定的、与决策相关的预测的挑战,这对于有效的公共卫生 监测 和应对至关重要。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究主题包括来自公共卫生、应用数学、传染病 流行病学 和微生物科学的 22 篇贡献,涵盖 麻疹、流感、登革热和其他公共卫生关注的疾病。
elements_zh.methods: 该研究主题涵盖机械建模、统计预测、机器学习、随机优化、计算流体动力学和负担分析,重点是将这些方法整合到不同的疾病和环境中。
elements_zh.main_results: 研究表明,当适当考虑非线性和特定地点的影响时,背景协变量可以加强当地早期预警和风险分层,并且铁路连通性与 COVID-19 的早期城际传播有关。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,干预措施必须根据连通性结构进行定制,例如铁路网络、建筑物和社会联系,这些结构创造了独特的 传播 路径。这凸显了对上下文敏感建模和分析的需求。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果为开发更准确的 监测 工具提供了信息,并强调了整合环境、社会经济和卫生系统数据以改善公共卫生决策的重要性。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 证据是中等的,因为它是基于一系列研究而不是单一的、集中的实验,并且结果的普遍性取决于所使用的具体背景和数据源。

analysis_zh.main_results: 研究表明,当适当考虑非线性和特定地点的影响时,背景协变量可以加强当地早期预警和风险分层,并且铁路连通性与 COVID-19 的早期城际传播有关。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,干预措施必须根据连通性结构进行定制,例如铁路网络、建筑物和社会联系,这些结构创造了独特的 传播 路径。这凸显了对上下文敏感建模和分析的需求。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果为开发更准确的 监测 工具提供了信息,并强调了整合环境、社会经济和卫生系统数据以改善公共卫生决策的重要性。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 证据是中等的,因为它是基于一系列研究而不是单一的、集中的实验,并且结果的普遍性取决于所使用的具体背景和数据源。
